speechtext:
Before we go into
supply I want to take a few minutes, Mr. 
Speaker, to protest the removal by the Department of Trade and Commerce of the restrictions governing the export of fish livers, particularly to the United States. The restrictions which have been in effect over the last ten years have built up extracting plants on the British Columbia coast. Now the raw product is being allowed to go across the border into the United States, and these industries are in danger. The industry was not forewarned of this step, and repercussions will be serious, especially among the fishermen and their co-operatives. The people involved in the industry want the restrictions put on again.
A little while ago we listened to the requests of the canning companies and put restrictions on the export of raw salmon going into the United States. It seems that these same companies are not protesting the lifting of the restrictions on fish livers, but others interested in the industry are vitally concerned. I believe the government should reconsider its plan and not knuckle under to this thing known as the Geneva trade agreement. which will completely ruin the fishing industry on the Pacific coast if affairs continue as they have been drifting. I would ask the government to reconsider its stand and again put into effect the laws governing the export of raw liver to the United States.

maintopic: EXPORT OF FISH LIVERS-DISTRIBUTION OF NAILS -BRITISH MARKET FOR B.C. APPLES
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I should like to add a word to what has been said by the hon. member for Skeena. I am amazed that such an order should have been issued by the Minister of Trade and Commerce, or by anyone else, without giving British Columbia some hint of what was being done. I certainly appreciate the many problems that come before the Minister of Trade and Commerce. I am sure that many hon. members would be glad of the opportunity to assist him in any way they could. I am amazed to have learned of this order from the hon. member for Skeena. It is most unfortunate that we did not have an opportunity to discuss the matter with the minister before the order was issued.

speechtext:
Before we go into supply, sir, I should like to raise a question arising out of a news item which appeared in the Winnipeg Tribune of May 15, which is headlined. ''Builders charge 'racket' in nails," This news item goes on to say:
A grey market and racket in distribution and sale of nails in the city was charged Friday by the Winnipeg housebuilders association.
I want to make it clear that I am not on this occasion speaking on behalf of the housebuilders association. I am not in a position

Distribution of Nails
to know whether the charges which are being made are based entirely upon facts. But the charges are so serious and the nail situation is so serious across the country that the government at the earliest opportunity, preferably today, should make some statement as to what steps are being taken in the matter. The charges of this association may be summarized in the following points: the nail shortage has reached alarming proportions; it is seriously restricting the construction of houses in Winnipeg; the prices of nails are excessive; certain organizations apparently have cornered the nail market, and the same situation exists in other cities across Canada.
If even a few of these five charges are coirect-if the prices being charged are excessive, if there is profiteering in the business of distributing nails, and if the situation is as serious as is pointed out in this news item, then the government should take immediate steps to remedy the situation.
I should like to quote further from this news item. The association deplored the activities of-

"certain organizations" which hail "apparently secured a corner on nails and, for the sake of a quick profit, are making the public pay . . ."
We have a prices committee which is delving into matters of the kind, and I think this emphasizes the utter futility of a committee sitting while prices soar. If the government are serious about this matter of prices, I would say that with the information that is coming out in the public press and what has already been brought out by .the prices committee, they have enough material and enough grounds now to move in the direction of setting prices right.
Here are some figures, and the government should let us know today whether they are correct. We are told that United States nails are quoted at $8 a keg f.o.b. shipping point, plus 55 cents for duty and freight, which makes them $8.55; but in Winnipeg the purchasers of nails are being charged from $12.50 to $13.50 a keg. which leaves a profit of $5 on each keg.
The association says this-and we should also know whether it is true:
"All appeals to the government, the manufacturers and the wholesalers seem to fall on deaf ears," the association says.
Apparently representations have been made, and no satisfactory reply has been given. Then there is this statement which is very direct, and it is a serious charge if it is true:
We are the victims of a racket in the distribution of nails. Unfortunately, this racket
seems to be within the law, but it is high time the government stepped in and made an investigation.
Further down it states that nails, on what is called the grey market, are available at from $15 to $18 a keg, which is almost double the regular price.

Mr. Speaker, with reference to the views expressed by the hon. member for Skeena (Mr. Archibald) and the hon. member for Comox-Alberni (Mr. Gibson), may I say, in reply to any opposition expressed to the action taken by the oil controller or the fisheries department in allowing fish livers to be exported to the United States, that such action meets with the approval of every fisherman in the maritime provinces. It meets with their approval for this reason. During the year 1947, fish livers in Canada, on the border where I live, were selling at four cents a pound in Canada, while in Maine they sold at eight cents a pound. The fishermen were compelled to sell to Canadian processors. The oils were purchased for the large drug companies in Canada, and after refining the oil they were allowed to ship it into the United States and take advantage of the high price of cod oil there, at the expense of the fishermen.
I can assure the wartime prices and trade board or the fisheries department, or whoever is responsible for the action taken, that it has the wholehearted support of every fisherman in my riding, and, I believe, in the maritime provinces.

Mr. Speaker, I should like to say a word in support of the remarks made by the hon. member for Dauphin (Mr. Zaplitny). I believe a protest has been made by the Federated Co-operatives of Saskatchewan, who are unable to get steel rods for the manufacture of nails. I understand that

complaint is being made to the combines investigation officers, and certain correspondence which I have seen has been or will be forwarded to them. That, I believe, indicates clearly that the large steel companies of Canada do not wish to supply nails to new customers of the type of the Federated Co-operatives of Saskatchewan.
Seventy-five thousand members of the federated co-operatives rely for their basic supplies nowadays mainly on the society itself, and every attempt has been made to supply the farmers with nails, not only for the building of homes, barns, granaries and so on, but also for such uses as those to which the hon. member for Dauphin referred.
I rise to ask the minister to look into the matter of a suspected combine in connection with the manufacture of nails and the distribution of steel generally, because I believe that the steel companies of Canada do constitute a virtual monopoly in the production of some of these commodities and are able to decide who shall distribute them. That is against the spirit at least of the legislation now in effect in Canada, and I support the hon. member for Dauphin and ask the government to look into the phase of the situation which I have mentioned.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to bring to the attention of the house a serious grievance on the part of the registered apple growers of British Columbia. I mentioned this matter a few nights ago, and since I spoke on that occasion the growers in my constituency have held a meeting and are protesting strongly against the loss of the British preference. Furthermore, they have passed a resolution in which they indicate their willingness to take British securities and sterling in payment for their apples. The apple growers in the Okanagan in British Columbia are also considering the same approach.
Some of the growers in my district are willing to take British securities in payment for their apples, but we have been told that the British market is not now available or worth considering. I trust the Minister of Trade and Commerce will give his attention to what I am saying.
As a matter of fact, Great Britain has been importing large quantities of apples from Australia, Tasmania and New Zealand, and as late as March 15 the British government made an offer for the purchase of 500,000 boxes of apples from Belgium and Holland, but without success. We believe that some arrangement could be made whereby our growers would be enabled to ship to Great Britain certain

British Market for B.C. Apples
varieties which are in short supply there. Dessert apples are not grown in quantities in Great Britain. In fact, dessert apples are generally off the market about the end of December. I urge the Minister of Trade and Commerce and the Minister of Finance to give this matter their serious attention. When these growers are willing to take sterling and British securities in payment, I submit that under the circumstances their views and suggestions should receive every consideration.
May I indicate to the minister the position so far as gift apples to Great Britain are concerned. Prior to the war we were in the habit of shipping from British Columbia hundreds of carloads to Great Britain. The apples were assembled in the Okanagan and Kootenay and then shipped to the old country for delivery to the customer by carriers. That is not possible at the present time. The matter was taken up with the food minister, Mr. Strachey, who advised that the apples could be sent in bulk. We could send carload lots, 750 boxes to the car, provided we shipped to the British ministry of food without designating the recipients, and the ministry w'ould distribute the apples as they saw fit.
I suggest that the Minister of Trade and Commerce take the matter up with the British officials. Many. Canadians are prepared to pay for gift apples to Great Britain. This year we could send overseas as gifts to Britain between 300,000 and 500,000 boxes of apples- don't forget 500,000 boxes of apples represents 606 carloads. I should perhaps say just a word particularly about nails. The production of nails has been increasing each month. Distribution is carefully watched. The price of the Canadian product is a stable price. The price at the mill is kept in proportion with the price of basic steel. I think it is a credit to the industry, and perhaps to the government, that the steel industry has not responded to the urgent demand but rather has kept a stable price. The pattern of distribution has been most carefully watched. Full protection is given to the building of low-cost houses. Under any government housing plan, nails are given complete priority. Nails have been going into essential houses to the full extent required.
It has been suggested that there is a monopoly in nail wire. I wish there were more nail wire; then there might be an excuse for a monopoly. The position is this-and I will speak of the Steel Company of Canada as an example. The Steel Company of Canada have $90,000,000 invested in facilities for making basic and finished steel. They draw the wire and they have nail machines. They make nails. Those nail machines are running at only about sixty per cent capacity. Why? Because the demand for their wire for various uses-baling, barbed wire and agricultural uses; it is used largely in making agricultural implements-leaves only so much
Distribution oj Nails

wire to be put into nails. The same is true at Dosco, which also has a large investment in primary facilities and in nail making machinery. Those two firms make, I suppose, seventy-five per cent of the nails in Canada. There is a firm on the Pacific coast-the name escapes me at the moment-which has been a traditional customer of Dosco for nail wire, and the requirements of that firm have been protected. There may be two or three other small users, and their requirements have been protected. They were part of the prewar pattern of distribution, and that has been maintained. It is not a matter of shortage in any one locality; if there is a shortage, it is a shortage which is pretty well uniform across Canada, because the pattern of the distribution of nails has been carefully watched.

I want to ask the minister just one question. Mr. Speaker, Bill E5, an act to amend the Canada Shipping Act, which has come
Canada Shipping Act

from the other place, contains a number of amending sections to the present Canada Shipping Act. The Canada Shipping Act was passed in 1934, proclaimed in 1936, amended twice thereafter, and this group of sections which the house has before it now seeks further to amend it.
The Canada Shipping Act, 1934, is divided into sixteen different parts, each of which deals with separate and various aspects of maritime law. The amendments contained in this bill cover certain miscellaneous matters, and in the main the bill may be considered under five headings. The first has to do with certification of officers, the second with shipping of seamen, the third with steamship inspection, the fourth with a new section to the act, fatal accidents, and the fifth with the approval of certain international conventions which were passed at Seattle in 1947.
I should like to deal with these five sections of the bill seriatim. Part II of the act is designed to provide that all ships shall have properly qualified officers and masters, mates and engineers. Owing to the prevailing scarcity of qualified deck officers and engineers, the government considers it advisable to permit relaxation to be made in the requirements of sections 113 and 114, which have to do with the number of qualified masters, mates and engineers there should be on each ship, and also with respect to sections 132 and 133 of the act, which have to do with the clearance of ships at customs.
The house will remember that under the Was Measures Act, during the war years, there was passed order in council P.C. 4306 of June 17, 1941. This order gave the minister concerned permission to grant to any Canadian registered ship the right to clear on a voyage, even though the master or mate of such ship has a certificate a grade lower than that required by the Canada Shipping Act, 1934, and it also gave the minister some power with reference to second, third or fourth-class engineers, so that these could be substituted in place of first, second or third-class engineers.
This order in council, as the house will recall, was passed under the War Measures Act and continued under the transitional powers act, this year continued until the end of March, 1949. It is proposed to insert practically the same language in the act under section 133 (A), which will authorize the minister to exempt any ship from any requirement contained in sections 113,114,132 and 133, or to dispense with the observance of any such requirement under certain conditions and subject to certain safeguards.

I should like to draw the attention of the house to the fact that the same position obtains in the United Kingdom where section 78 of the Merchant Shipping Act, 1906, gives the board of trade, now the ministry of transport, power to exempt any ship from any requirement of the Merchant Shipping Act, or to dispense with the observance of any such requirement. It is considered, in the interests of the maritime industry of this country, and in order to keep ships moving, that this section is of the utmost importance, and it is hoped that, in order to keep our ships moving, the house will give approval to this section, which exempts the certification of officers, masters and engineers from the requirements of the sections I have mentioned.
There are proposed in the bill other amendments having to do with the certification of officers, but I shall not take up the time of the house by dealing with them at this stage.
The second part to which I should like to draw the attention of the house is that having to do with seamen. Part III, of the Canada Shipping Act provides for the shipping of seamen and the rights and liabilities of seamen, and provision is made in great detail. Seamen on inland waters are differentiated in some respects from those who sail the deep seas.
This part of the act contains special provisions for the protection of seamen, who as a class have always been regarded as favourites of the law. The government has given the most- careful consideration to various representations made on behalf of seamen and has decided that certain provisions of part III should be amended so as to bring the act more into line with modern conditions of employment of seamen.
Various amendments are proposed to part III, the most important of which is, I think, contained in the clause of the bill which provides for giving legislative effect to four international conventions.

maintopic: CANADA SHIPPING ACT AMENDMENTS TO ACT OF 1934
speechtext: What clause?

maintopic: CANADA SHIPPING ACT AMENDMENTS TO ACT OF 1934
speechtext:
Clause 228 (A) of the act. These international conventions have to do with the medical examination of seafarers, certification of ships' cooks, catering and food supply on board ship, and the certification also of able-bodied seamen. I wish to refer to these conventions more in detail as I go along, particularly when I reach that part of the bill.
There is provision in the bill for the appointment of shipping masters, which provision I think will commend itself to the house. As the house knows, shipping masters are now

Canada Shipping Act
appointed by the governor in council and are paid fees of office in lieu of salary. It is proposed from now on to appoint them in the regular way under the Civil Service Act and we intend to pay them by salary.
Section 222 of the act provides for the disposition of the property of deceased seamen. The section as it now stands has been found cumbersome and has created difficulties from time to time for the dependents of seamen who have claimed assets. The amendment as proposed will facilitate the disposal of wages and effects of deceased seamen.

maintopic: CANADA SHIPPING ACT AMENDMENTS TO ACT OF 1934
speechtext: What section?

maintopic: CANADA SHIPPING ACT AMENDMENTS TO ACT OF 1934
speechtext:
Section 222. The government recognizes the importance of the galley in the life and work of a seaman, and provision is made in the bill to require foreign-going ships of 1,000 tons or over to carry certificated cooks. One of the international labour organization's conventions set out in the schedule to the bill also makes provision for the certification of ships' cooks, but as this convention depends upon other nations for ratification, it has been considered advisable to legislate independently of the convention, so that there shall be no delay in requiring Canadian ships of this class to carry certified cooks.
I might also mention the amendment to section 244 of the act, which abolishes the penalty of imprisonment for desertion or for being absent without leave in Canada. This is a new departure. As the law now stands, when a seaman deserts his ship he is liable not only to forfeiture but also to proceedings leading to imprisonment. If this amendment is accepted by the house there will be no longer the penalty of imprisonment for seamen who desert their ship or who are absent without leave from their ship in Canada. In so far as that convention is concerned, outside Canada, the position remains exactly as it was.

maintopic: CANADA SHIPPING ACT AMENDMENTS TO ACT OF 1934
speechtext: May I ask if that refers just to foreign ships?

maintopic: CANADA SHIPPING ACT AMENDMENTS TO ACT OF 1934
speechtext:
No. That refers to all ships. While still dealing with the question of desertion, I should like to point out to the house that there is no imprisonment for desertion in the United Kingdom. The bill provides for a new subsection 2 which is added to section 244, the desertion section, which explains and makes clear that a seaman who is on strike cannot be guilty of desertion. It is therein set out that a seaman is not guilty of an offence under section 244 by reason only of the fact that he has taken part in a lawful strike after his ship has been placed in security at a port in Canada.
In the other place an amendment has been made to this section as well as to several others, and I should like to take a moment or two to deal with those when I have completed my remarks.
A third part with which this bill deals has to do with steamship inspection. Part VII of the act covers steamship inspection; and a number of important amendments contained in the bill deal with that part. Provision is made, for example, for the inspection of classed ships; that is to say, ships which are classed with an approved classification society such as Lloyd's, or British Corporation, at longer intervals than one year. The act now provides for annual inspection of steamships; that is section 387. Representations have been made that classed ships are inspected annually by classification society-surveyors, which involves a duplication of steamship inspection. Those representations went on to say that a complete inspection requiring drydocking of the vessel, by a Canadian steamship inspector, should not be required every year. The government considers that the steamship inspection requirements for classed ships should be modified and be more in line with classification rules. The amendment to section 387 provides for the inspection of classed ships at longer intervals than once in a year, as the governor in council may prescribe. It is not intended, however, to relieve classed ships from annual inspection in respect of lifesaving and fire-extinguishing equipment.
There are other important amendments contained in the bill which affect part VII. For instance, clause I contains the definition of "pleasure yacht", which makes it clear that such a vessel cannot be used to carry passengers as a matter of business and retain its status as a pleasure yacht exempt from annual inspection and the requirements of the act relating to the carrying of certificated officers. This amendment is brought about by a series of accidents which took place on the lakes, and on Georgian bay particularly, in pleasure yachts which did not follow the provisions of this section. It has been found necessary to amend the act accordingly.
The expression "sailing ship" is also defined to mean a ship wholly propelled by sails. Ships which are equipped with propelling machinery, even though they are also equipped with sails, will become subject to steamship inspection and the requirements of the act respecting competency of officers.
Some years ago a commission was set up by the government to deal with the operation of small boats on the river St. Lawrence, and one of the recommendations brought in by the
Canada Shipping Act

then commissioner, Hon. Mr. Justice Lucien Cannon, District Judge in Admiralty of the Exchequer Court of Canada, had to do with this particular matter. It has been thought advisable to amend the particular provision of the Canada Shipping Act having to do with small boats. I hope that amendment will commend itself to the house.
Another important amendment relating to steamship inspection included in the bill again has to do with one of the orders in council that was passed under the War Measures Act. This was order in council P.C. 2245 of March 23, 1942, which authorized the chairman of the board of steamship inspection to relieve ships from inspection requirements in any specific case of emergency where he deemed it necessary or advisable in the public interest, to such extent, in such manner and upon such terms as after investigation the circumstances warranted. It was provided that the chairman of the steamship inspection board could not relieve any ship or any owner of such ship from the requirements of part VII of the act until and unless the ship was in seaworthy condition. That order in council was extended under the transitional powers act, and further extended this session until March, 1949. Thanks to this section, during the war years the steamship inspection board were able to assist where action was required in great haste, without amending the act. It is proposed to continue the provision or the principle contained in that order in council with some slight changes in one of the amending sections. It will be under section 488A, which will authorize the minister, on the recommendation of the chairman of the board of steamship inspection, to relieve ships from complying with part VII of the act in specific cases of emergency as therein more specifically set out. I have referred already to the Merchant Shipping Act, 1906, of the United Kingdom, which gave the ministry of transport power to dispense with the observance of any requirement of the Merchant Shipping Acts. This amendment will be in line with a similar section or one very much like it now in existence in the United Kingdom act.
Then I come to the next part with which the bill deals, and that has to do with fatal accidents. It is a new part altogether. It is introduced under the heading "Fatal Accidents." At present there is no provision in the act that entitles the dependents of deceased persons killed as a result of an injury caused by a ship to take proceedings in rem against the ship. A seaman can always go into the admiralty court and sue the ship or elect to take compensation under the

provincial workmen's compensation acts or under the dominion act which was passed recently in this House of 'Commons. But heretofore the dependents have not had the right to take action against the ship, what is called an action in rem. This new section will entitle the dependents of a deceased seaman to institute such an action, or to elect to take compensation, whichever is the higher or whichever they prefer. It has been held that the exchequer court on its admiralty side has no jurisdiction to entertain an action in rem in respect of fatal accidents; and the provisions of this part are intended to remedy this defect, in the law and to enable dependents of deceased persons to take proceedings in the court of admiralty in any case where the deceased person would have had the right to maintain an action if death bad not ensued. The provisions and terms of this new part are very similar to -those contained in the fatal accidents acts of the provinces, -particularly the act in Ontario.
The last part with which this bill concerns itself is the international labour conventions. In the schedule to the bill are set out four international labour conventions which the government proposes to ratify and make effective by regulations of the governor in council. These conventions, as I have already stated, are: the medical examination (seafarers) convention, 1946; the certification of able seamen convention, 1946; food and catering (ships' crews) convention, 1946, and the certification of ships' cooks convention, 1946.
The convention concerning the medical examination of seafarers provides that no person shall be engaged for employment in a seagoing vessel unless he holds a medical certificate attesting to his fitness for the work for which he is employed. In the convention are set out the various conditions and the various ships to which the convention does not apply; for instance, certain small seagoing vessels of less than two hundred tons gross registered tonnage, certain fishing vessels, estuarial craft and the like are not subject to this convention. It also provides for each government to prescribe the nature of the examination and the manner in which the medical examination shall be held, together with the particulars to be included in the medical certificate, as well as the period during which the certificate shall remain in force. The medical examination of seamen is not provided for in any part of the Canada Shipping Act as it now stands.
The next convention, dealing with the certification of able seamen, provides that no person

Canada Shipping Act
shall be engaged on any vessel as an able seaman unless he holds a certificate of qualification stating that he is competent to perform any duty which may be required of a member of a crew serving in the deck department. This convention also provides that each government shall make arrangements for the holding of examinations and the granting of certificates of qualification. It also provides that no person shall be granted a certificate unless he has reached the minimum age, which is eighteen years, unless he has served at sea for a certain length of time and unless he has passed an examination of proficiency, and that the minimum period of service at sea, generally speaking, shall be not less than three years. The certification of able seamen, like the medical certification, is not required under the existing provisions of the Canada Shipping Act. As it now stands, that act only provides that a seaman shall not be entitled to the rating of able-bodied seaman unless he has served three years at sea.
The third1 convention concerns food and catering for crews on board ship. It provides for the promotion of a proper standard of food supply and catering service for the crews of seagoing vessels that are engaged in the transport of cargo and passengers for the purpose of trade. The convention contains many provisions designed to ensure a proper food supply and catering service for seamen on seagoing vessels.
Finally, the certification of ships' cooks convention provides that no person shall be engaged as ship's cook on a seagoing vessel unless he holds a certificate of qualification, and that each government shall make arrangements for the holding of examinations and for the granting of certificates. The existing provisions of the Canada Shipping Act do not require certificated ships' cooks.
I should add that these four conventions apply to seagoing ships and would not affect the operation of ships which ply on inland waters, except possibly with respect to the engagement of an able seaman, if an inland water sailor wished to be rated as an ablebodied seaman.
Before leaving this part of my remarks, I should like to deal briefly with the amendments made in the other place, which I am sure will be given careful consideration by the house. With but one exception I think there is no serious effect on any principle laid down in the act. The clauses having to do with the definition of home trade, inland waters and minor waters have been extended to a certain degree and, as I stated a moment ago in connection with section 244, which provides that a seaman who is on strike is not deemed to be a
deserter within the meaning of that section, the other place has seen fit to amend the provision by further defining the terms and conditions under which a ship must be safely placed at harbour. Perhaps I might read this amendment, because I consider it of some importance :
A seaman is not guilty of an offence under this section by reason only of his taking part in a lawful strike after his ship and cargo have been placed in security to the satisfaction of the harbour master or the master of the ship where no harbour master is available, at the terminal port in Canada of the voyage in which the ship is engaged.
I should think that amendment would add considerably to the value of the subsection.
Then it was deemed advisable to amend section 482 (1) of the act, which provides for continuous discharge books in a form to be approved by the minister. The house may have some reservations with respect to that amendment. Certain amendments were added in order to come to the assistance of pilots on the St. Lawrence river, and on the whole I believe those amendments should commend themselves to the house. Other amendments are of a minor nature, and I do not propose to deal with them at this time.
In this brief review of this important bill I have endeavoured to outline the main and cardinal points with which the house will be asked to deal in these amendments. The Canada Shipping Act requires a good deal of study for one to be familiar with its many and varied provisions which constitute the basis of our maritime law.
In conclusion, may I say that the government has considered carefully the representations made by organizations interested in the welfare of our merchant marine and the seamen who man the ships. I do not think this act is one which should be changed drastically as some would advocate. It is a result of many years of experience in the operation of merchant ships, which is different from any other kind of transportation. The experience of the years should not lightly be cast aside if the shipping industry of this country is to prosper. The amendments contained in bill E5 are designed to strengthen this industry and to help the seamen who go down to the sea in ships flying the Canadian flag.

maintopic: CANADA SHIPPING ACT AMENDMENTS TO ACT OF 1934
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as a former chairman of the harbour board of the city of Toronto, and one who has given much thought and attention to the Canada Shipping Act, I am surprised that on this eighty-fifth day of the session the minister should bring down a bill of this kind, particularly when we realize that we shall be here fos
Canada Shipping Act

only about six weeks more. In this short time he asks the house to pass these amendments to the Canada Shipping Act.
Let me say that these amendments constitute virtually a new shipping act for Canada. First, it changes the definition of a ship. Formerly (he definition stated that any craft not propelled by oars was a ship. Now pleasure boats, and other craft of that kind, have been added.
In my view this bill should have been submitted to the marine sections of boards of trade in Canada. Hon. members are aware that shipping on tlhe lakes is a precarious business, to the point where there have been mergers of passenger and cargo shipping interests. Even yet they are having considerable trouble.
The time for a proper shipping act is long overdue, for the protection of those who sail the ships in all kinds of weather, from the upper lakes down to the sea, so as to advance the grain trade and the western crop to the seaboard.
In my view this bill should be sent to a committee. I sympathize fully with the difficulties which have confronted both the Minister of Labour (Mr. Mitchell) and the Minister of Transport (Mr. Ohevrier) in recent months. I have seen some of the dhips operating on the lakes, and I know something about the conditions under which labour operates on those lakes today. They risk their lives, and in the event of difficulty, through storms, United States lifesaving stations have to come into action.
The bill proposes to read into the statute another labour convention. For the first time, so far as I know, a difference is made between the granting of a certificate for a cargo ship and for a passenger ship. The governor in council, through the minister, has power to grant certain temporary certificates to mates, captains and other ship officials. All officers who are of the rank of lieutenants in the Canadian Navy have the right to operate a ship on the ocean or lakes, for purposes of domestic trade. This feature, I believe, goes a little too far, unless it can be Shown that these officers have had experience in the handling of passenger or cargo ships at sea.
Today the admiralty court meets but seldom, at which time it goes across Canada. In Ontario we have only one admiralty judge who, I am pleased to say, is a good one. It will be noticed, however, that if there is a fatal accident on a cargo or passenger ship the case is tried by the admiralty judge, whereas formerly suit could be brought in the assizes, as the latter courts meet three
(Mr. Church.]
or four times a year and the admiralty court only on special work.
This would appear to be a satisfactory bill in many ways; but there are other features of it which in my view should receive careful consideration before, on this eighty-fifth day of the session, we are asked to accept it.
Some other changes, all of which I shall not outline, have been made. Some of these deal with the definitions of officers of ships, and others relate to the powers of the minister. We know that formerly, until 1936, a minister of marine was in charge of the department. That work is now done by the Department of Transport; and in my view this was a proper change.
So far as rates are concerned, hon. members know that water-borne traffic on the inland lakes has, in the past, had the effect of regulating rail freight rates. I am sorry to say that on Lake Ontario and Lake Erie we have lost some of the passenger ships which formerly helped to regulate freight rates during the spring and summer months. I have in mind particularly boats which operated between Toronto and the towns and cities of Picton, Belleville, Trenton, Brighton, Colborne, Port Hope, Cobourg, Whitby and Oshawa. Those boats were effective in bringing the crops and package freight to Toronto during the summer months. We know, too, that an average of about 800,000 tons of coal a year is brought by ship to Ashbridge's bay and the ship channel at Toronto, as was seen the other day by those members who visited that city. That coal comes in part from lake Ontario and lake Erie ports, and is a great boon to our city.
While the bill has many good features, I hope the minister will see fit to have it referred to a committee of the house. It is one of the most important bills we have had before parliament in the last twelve or fourteen years. I remember when it was proposed in the Armstrong bill that jurisdiction over freight rates on the lakes should be placed in the hands of the boards of transport commissioners or, as it was then known, the board of railway commissioners. The proposal was opposed for years by the shipping interests on the lakes, deputations appeared before the select committee and supported Mr. J. E. Armstrong, member for Lambton-Kent of that day, and asked that the board be empowered to regulate freight and passenger rates on inland waters.
It will be noted that the bill makes reference to minor waters. As described in the bill, these would not include lakes Ontario, Erie, Huron and Superior, and Georgian bay. I

Canada Shipping Act
believe lake Winnipeg is included. There are, however, many other important navigable streams and rivers in the country which, due to the development of water power, and the possible development in the future, will be of great importance.
In the early days transportation was by canoe. Parkman states that no cape was entered or river turned unless a canoe led the way. Those were the days of pioneer civilization. From that day we see how we have become the fifth trading nation in the world.
I would repeat my view that not only should this bill be sent to the various boards of trade, labour organizations and others, but should be placed before a committee of the house. We are reading into the bill certain conventions agreed to by international labour groups. I have nothing in particular to say about that, except that anything we accept should be adapted to our circumstances. I have read some of the provisions; conditions in Canada should be kept in mind, and it should be remembered that our conditions are not those of South American and other countries where they have water-borne traffic twelve months of the year. Ours is only seasonal traffic, and provision should be made along those lines. I suggest that this bill be advanced a stage and then sent to a committee of the house, because six weeks is too short a time for this house to draft a brand new shipping act. The last amendment was in 1934, when the bill was sent to a committee presided over by the Hon. Mr. Cahan.
This is a most important bill. We want to encourage water-borne traffic and regulate freight and passenger rates on ships. We are a nautical people, and we never should have the trouble we are having with our seamen on the great lakes. Nothing has done more for Canada than our aquatic sports. Ned Hanlon spread the name of Canada far and wide when he went to Australia. Gordon on the Nile had to get loggers from Canada to navigate those waters. The youth of this country are interested in aquatics. Canada's navy made a glorious record in the late war and proved a blessing to this country. Many of our Canadian youth who served in the navy as able-bodied seamen would like to join the shipping industry on the great lakes, and it could provide a great deal of work for them. I hope that the bill will be advanced a stage and then be sent to a committee of this house for study.

maintopic: CANADA SHIPPING ACT AMENDMENTS TO ACT OF 1934
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to make a few comments on the amendments to the Canada Shipping Act. I am pleased to see some of the improvements made; for example, shipping masters are to be in the position of civil servants. I have had representations both from the union to which I belong and from businessmen in the city of Prince Rupert asking that this be done. If the shipping master in such a port as Prince Rupert were to leave the port, there would be nobody else there qualified for the post; yet this man has a necessary function to perform. I hope that such a man as we have in Prince Rupert will be included in the civil service, as this gentleman is performing a very necessary function.
The amendments also make certain improvements in regard to health and the certification of such trades as cooks. One thing I did not understand in the original amendments, and I presume it is in the new amendments which were placed before us just before this debate opened. The original bill laid down certain qualifications for a certified cook. Yet when it comes to the certification of an able seaman we are referred to the schedule which is, I presume, to be brought into force by order in council.

maintopic: CANADA SHIPPING ACT AMENDMENTS TO ACT OF 1934
speechtext: May I explain? The international conventions were approved by members of the I.L.O. Four of them were approved. The reason why my hon. friend sees a repetition in the bill of ship's cook is that it may take some years, or at least some months, before the convention is approved. That is the reason for putting it in the bill.

maintopic: CANADA SHIPPING ACT AMENDMENTS TO ACT OF 1934
speechtext:
I hope that the government can act speedily and, of course, with justice to see that the seamen are given certification and that certain qualifications are demanded of them. In the briefs that I have received from the Seafarers' International Union they have asked for that. I imagine that the government have been forced to this conclusion by the fact that they had to lower the qualifications for officers. A seaman's job used to be anyone's job who would come into a port and go out on a boat. I hope that there will be stricter regulations governing shipping in the coastwise trade to provide that they must carry a good number of able seamen and other trades so that we can begin to build up the occupation of seafarer.
I am sorry that the eight-hour day has not been incorporated in the bill. I sat on a board of arbitration drawing up agreements between the Seafarers' International Union, the Canadian Pacific, the Canadian National, and Union Steamships on the coast, and a lot of discussion was caused because the eight-hour day was not enforced on shipping. Union Steamships has stops at inaccessible places
Canada Shipping Act

and more is demanded of the men who work for that company. I imagine it boils down to this, that the rates will have to go up or more subsidies be paid. But it all comes out of the hide of the average seaman, and we would like to see the eight-hour day established. Furthermore the present situation is not a healthy one. There is in Vancouver, for example, the local office of the union. Many of the old-timers will be waiting around there until a United States boat comes in. They do not want to go out on a Canadian boat. My own brother was forced into that position. He took a voyage on a United States boat because he would make more money and work under better conditions on a ship flying the United States flag. The navigation laws of the United States are much more advanced than ours, and we could have gone quite a bit farther than we are doing in these amendments.
The seamen would like to have the advance note system abolished. That is a system under which the skipper has the power to advance on the man's wages one pound per week while he is in port. The seamen would like to have that changed to the corresponding item in the navigation laws of the United States, where they have what is called a slop chest, and the seaman is not forced to take a note to a beer parlour or a restaurant and have it discounted, but he can buy what he wants on board, tobacco, clothing, and so forth, and at a reasonable price. That is the system on United States vessels but not on Canadian vessels to any great extent.
I was disappointed that the other place in its wisdom turned down the representations made by the Department of Transport that the continuous discharge book be done away with. I do not know what these men are thinking of in the other place when they do that sort of thing.

maintopic: CANADA SHIPPING ACT AMENDMENTS TO ACT OF 1934
speechtext: They are not thinking at all.

maintopic: CANADA SHIPPING ACT AMENDMENTS TO ACT OF 1934
speechtext: I would give them the benefit of the doubt.

maintopic: CANADA SHIPPING ACT AMENDMENTS TO ACT OF 1934
speechtext: That is very hard.

maintopic: CANADA SHIPPING ACT AMENDMENTS TO ACT OF 1934
speechtext:
Take the position of seamen today. They are our representatives in foreign ports, and we want the best type we can get. We want stable labour relations, but we cannot have them with this sort of thing. Even if a man is a perfectly good seaman, he may get a skipper with whom he does not get along, and he is tagged from then on. He has a bad record stamped right in his book. These men want to be treated as ordinary
IMr. Archibald.]
civilian workers, not as slaveys. This is not the good old days of the British navy at the time of Trafalgar. You cannot expect to impose conditions such as that. It is erroneous to believe that you can get the best types by maintaining such conditions and a continuous discharge book by which a man's record can be brought up against him even though he has made only one mistake. Because of the continuous discharge book, he will be hung with that mistake for the rest of his life.
In addition, the nature of the trade is different from what it was in the old days when men were gone for a year or more. We are now living in the age of steam, turbines, diesel engines and so on, and voyages are not of too long duration. Men can usually sail into a major port where all grievances are straightened out by business agents and so on. I should like to see the government lead off by ignoring the attitude of the other place and bringing in what the department asks for, and do away with the continuous discharge book.
Another point I should like to bring up at this time is the matter of shipwrecks. I notice that facilities for getting the men home have been improved, but if they lose all their effects they are not replaced. Men going to sea today take their radios along with them as well as electric shaving outfits, and so on. These things mean quite a bit to them. In the event of a shipwreck they lose all their gear. They are just given clothing if they require it when they get into some port where the port authorities can give it to them. The companies should carry insurance to pay for the loss of the effects of the men. The nature of the industry is not such that the men themselves can carry insurance. I have in my possession some correspondence which came to me a few years ago, and which dealt with the ship West Clark Park. The men lost all their effects off the coast of Mexico, but could not get any recompense. I have mentioned this before in the house. There was the case of the government's own snag boat on the Skeena river which was burnt. The men lost all their effects, and the department would not recompense them for their loss. That sort of thing should be cleared up through the medium of insurance for the men if they lost their effects. These are things that should be cleared up at this time.
I should like to mention one other thing.
I do not want to do it in a contentious way.
I bring it up because it comes under the Canada Shipping Act. I refer to the deep-

Supply-Transport
sea fishermen. On the west coast the government is actively sponsoring more and more deep-sea fishermen. In fact it has a boat going out on the Pacific to explore further development of tuna fishing or any other kind that can be developed with semi-oceangoing fishing boats. Take the halibut boats. They are fifty, sixty, and seventy feet long.

maintopic: CANADA SHIPPING ACT AMENDMENTS TO ACT OF 1934
speechtext: And whaling as well.

maintopic: CANADA SHIPPING ACT AMENDMENTS TO ACT OF 1934
speechtext:
Yes, the halibut fleet goes away up off the coast of Alaska most of the time. The tuna fleet goes down off the coast of California, Washington and Oregon most of the time. Under the act they pay a certain amount and are covered for health and accident, but they can get the benefits of that only in a Canadian port. The whole fishing fleet is going through an evolution. The boats are getting bigger and bigger and are going farther afield. We should like to see the act extended, so that these men would be covered when they were off the California coast or the Alaska coast and had to run into California, Ketchikan or Juneau or any of the ports off Alaska. It would not mean a great deal more expense. All the men are now paying into the fund. It would not mean extending it to other groups; it would mean that you would be extending the facilities to men who are already paying into the fund. It would mean that the men would be more prepared to take ventures and, believe me, in tuna fishing especially these men are taking ventures. It would assist in extending the industry and permit the Canadian fleet to get a greater share of the fishing off the Pacific coast, because they are working under enough handicaps at the present time without others being imposed.
I should have liked to see in this bill further regulations as to holidays and so on, but I am beginning to see that in this house you go only step by step, and I am beginning to adapt myself to that spirit. However, I should like to see the minister go a little faster than he is doing at the present time.
I bring these suggestions to the minister for his consideration. From the experience I have had with labour relations in the maritime field I believe that if we went a little further it would build up a stable merchant marine personnel which could be dealt with a great deal better than is being done at the present time. The labour department is having its troubles now, and I believe a great deal of that trouble could be eliminated if conditions were improved somewhat along the lines that they have in the United States.

Mr. Chairman, when we adjourned on Friday evening two questions were asked to which I promised to give attention. One was a series of questions by the hon. member for Saint John-Albert. I find that the answers to the questions which he asked appear on page 142 of the minutes and proceedings of the committee on railways and shipping, dated April 21, 1948. He asked this question: Suppose you did not reduce the rate to Portland, would it have affected your business, and to what extent? That information is now being compiled and I hope to be able to get it for the hon. gentleman.
The hon. member for Saskatoon City raised a number of questions having to do with traffic at Churchill. The position at Churchill is, I think, very good. The facilities which exist there at the moment are, to my mind, sufficient to cope with any business that offers. I had the good fortune of visiting Churchill during the summer months and I saw for myself what was there and what was to be expected. I need not repeat what I said at the time. I do not wish to delay my own estimates, but I think

Supply-Transport

I should say in a general way that the port facilities are as good, other things being equal, as the facilities of the national harbours board in any other port in Canada.
Then he dealt with domestic and ocean rates. Let me at once dispose of ocean rates by telling him that the Department of Transport has no jurisdiction or control over those rates. They are not fixed by the government of Canada or by the department.
He also asked what the position was with reference to freight rates on the Hudson Bay railway. In the first place, as the hon. gentleman knows, the export and import rates on grains have not been increased, and that is by far the greatest amount of traffic that moves over the railway. Then, with reference to domestic rates, there are what are known as through rates and What are known as local rates. In so far as through rates are concerned, they have been increased by the railways, and they have been increased for this reason, that if a shipment of goods is moving, say, from Vancouver to Churchill, the rate is what is known as a through rate and it is subject to the 21 per cent increase ordered by the board. If it were otherwise, then it would be the addition of two local rates, namely the rate from Vancouver to The Pas plus the rate from The Pas to Churchill. The addition of those two local rates would be far greater than the 21 per cent increase, which would result in Churchill being discriminated1 against to a considerable extent.
With reference to the local rates, the present tariff on the Hudson Bay railway is what is known as the prairie scale. I am referring to the Canadian National Railways. The prairie scale in western Canada has been increased by 21 per cent. If it were not increased likewise on the Hudson Bay railway there could be a charge of discrimination against the rest of Canada in favour of the Hudson Bay railway.
I wish to make this further point. The Hudson bay route association have made very strong representations in favour of placing this railway under the jurisdiction of the board of transport commissioners and, if I am correct, I believe the hon. member for Saskatoon City made similar representations before the committee on railways and shipping last year. I think I should go further and say that not only the members of that association but also the railway brotherhoods in their presentation to the government this year asked that this railway be taken out of the description "under construction" and placed under the board of transport commissioners.

I have given instructions that that shall be done, and it will take some time before the actual transfer of jurisdiction is made.
These requests were made because the Hudson bay route association and particularly the brotherhoods thought it would be for the benefit and to the advantage of railway employees, and I believe the brotherhoods were right in that contention.
Strictly speaking, the position with reference to domestic rates is as I have stated. If the increase on the Hudson Bay railway had not been allowed to go into effect, jointly or concurrently with the increase in the rest of western Canada, a disastrous condition would have ensued for the export trade in the port of Churchill, and so far as traffic itself is concerned, which will be affected by the increase, I am informed it represents about eight per cent of the traffic that moves over the whole of the Hudson Bay railway.

I thank the minister for the courteous way in which he has given the information, and for the information itself. I hope it will clear up some of the difficulties under which the people out there have been labouring.
Before I sit down, I express the hope that this year the Hudson bay port will be given a test such as it deserves. I hope sufficient grain will be in position, so that a full quota of 15,000.000 or 20,000,000 bushels can be shipped from there, in order that we may for once have a test of this port to satisfy not only the people who use it but the people throughout the country; because at the present lime a good deal of the taxpayers' money is being put into that road and port, and there is no reason why it should not pay its own way.
There are other people as well as those intimately concerned who are interested in this port. The minister of co-operation in Saskatchewan, Mr. McIntosh, has been devoting a good deal of his attention to furthering the success of this road. Mr. Graham Spry, as trade agent of the Saskatchewan government in Britain is doing the same and is working up trade there. At a gathering of Canadian businessmen in London a short time ago a message was received from Sir Stafford Cripps himself, who expressed the hope that trade between Saskatchewan and British ports would be successful, and Mr. Dalgleish, president of the shipping company of the same name, is here in Canada at the moment, or is on his way here, to canvass for some of this trade which his boats may carry.

In conclusion, I believe that the attitude of the minister is favourable, and I say respectfully that I hope it will be more favourable than it once was, and that he and his government will give us an assurance of benevolent assistance in building up this trade, so that the greatest amount of lumber and wheat should go out this year, and that correspondingly greater imports of goods may be effected.

Mr. Chairman, I would not desire to take up the time of the committee but for the fact that my people in Peace River asked me to raise a question with the minister at this time in regard to the possibility of building an outlet to the coast from the Peace river country.
In the campaign of 1925 the Prime Minister promised an Edmonton audience that the Liberal party would make the Peace river country the spearhead for that party's development program. In the campaign of 1926 he told a similar audience in Edmonton that he would build the coast outlet for the Peace river country as soon as it was humanly possible. In the 1930 election campaign he again told an Edmonton audience that he would support the construction of a railway for the Peace river country within one year if the railway companies failed to build the coast outlet.
Of course the Liberal party was defeated in the campaign of 1930, and one can readily understand therefore why until 1935 the Prime Minister was not able to carry out his promise. But in this year 1948, after thirteen years of uninterrupted Liberal rule, the Peace river country is in much the same position, at least with regard to railroad transportation, as it was when the Prime Minister made his first promise back in 1925-26 and 1930. As a result, an estimated 100,000 people in the constituencies of Peace River and Cariboo- in one of the richest food-producing, lumber-producing and mineral-producing areas in all Canada, if not in North America-are carrying a transportation burden away beyond all reason. The last great undeveloped agricultural and mineral region of Canada is being greatly retarded in its development as a result of the failure of the Liberal party to keep its promises.
Moreover, it looks to me as if the railway companies of Canada have grown fat and lazy in their middle age. They have definitely lost the pioneering spirit which characterized their whole nature in the last years of the nineteenth century and the early years of the twentieth. In those earlier days they had 5849-254J
visions of what this great country could become and they drove ahead with their construction programs, fully confident that in due course within not too many years, the population would increase in these new areas; that people would come to settle the new country; that industry would develop; and that traffic would naturally surge upward, with that development and settlement, until their facilities would be taxed to capacity. Their faith and vision were justified.
In the past Canada has been good to the railroad companies; and I am wondering now, Mr. Chairman, if the railroads realize their obligations to the people of Canada. I should like to ask this question. Where is that pioneering spirit today? When one approaches the giant companies, grown fat and flabby, as I have approached them myself during the past two or three years with this problem of a coast outlet for the Peace river country, they seek refuge in an answer like this: well, as soon as the volume of traffic justifies it, we will build the outlet. To my mind, Mr. Chairman, that is nothing but pure evasion on their part. No one knows better than do the railroads that transportation and communication facilities must in large measure precede the development of a new area rather than follow it. That has been the history of the past, and it will be the history of the future. Where would the great wide open spaces of western Canada be today if the railroads, back in the days of the late nineties or the early nineteen-hundreds, had taken the same attitude as they take toward that great northwest today, namely, that the volume of traffic to a certain level must be provided before they will build roads or extend lines.
There is an argument, of course, that there is already a railroad into the Peace river country. I grant that. There is a line that penetrates from Edmonton for about 350 miles up into that great northwest, with a terminus on each side of the great Peace river, one at Hines Creek in Alberta on the north side and one at Dawson Creek on the south side of the river. But the traffic of the country is increasing greatly and the roads simply cannot handle the volume of traffic efficiently today, and at a cost the people can pay. The situation at the present time necessitates a long back haul. That is expensive for producers of grain, livestock and lumber, especially when it is remembered that, with the outlay of a moderate sum of money, an outlet could be provided to the west that would take off some 500 miles of necessary back haul of these great loads of produce. As we well know, the rates have been recently increased
Supply-Transport

and, as a result, have become more burdensome to the people in that area.
It seems to me that the building of the coast outlet should be undertaken at once. With its great areas of fertile lands, its timbered areas, its great coal fields-about which many hon. members know-which lie between Hudson Hope and Finlay Forks, its position as the gateway to the Northwest Territories where great mineral deposits have already been discovered and partly developed, the Peace river country could well support a population, I would judge, of from 300,000 to 400,000 people. Lately there has been discovered in the area sufficient waterpower to service a population of that number; that is, a population of between 300,000 and 400,000 people. This waterpower awaits development.
It is essential in the interests of a strong Canada that the great northwest be developed and populated at the earliest possible time. Twenty-three years ago the Prime Minister indicated that he realized how necessary such development was at that time. How much more essential is it now? I need not dwell at any great length on the world's need for food materials which that section of the country can produce, the minerals that the world needs which that area can produce, and the lumber which that area can produce in abundance. Nor do I need to take the time to describe the importance of the northwest from the point of view of the security of Canada; that is, from the military point of view.
I just want to say this. This great inland empire cannot play its part in building a strong Canada unless it is well provided with railway transportation. It seems to me that the logical thing to do would be for the government to adopt a program covering a period of years-let us say five years; you might call it their five-year northwest development program-that would result in providing a continuous railway line from Prince Albert, Saskatchewan, to Meadow Lake by way of Lac la Biche, through the Peace river country and on to the coast. Less than 500 miles of new construction would be required to provide such a northern route that would give a continuous and clear outlet from Prince Albert, Saskatchewan, to the Pacific coast. Such a road would serve northern Saskatchewan, the whole of the Athabaska country represented in this house by the hon. member for Athabaska (Mr. Dechene), the Peace river, the Cariboo and Skeena; it would help to develop a great empire and would contribute materially to the development of the coast ports.
Such a program could be taken in steps. It seems to me one step should be to push a

road through from Hines Creek to the coal fields at Hudson Hope, not a very great distance, making available the fine coal that can be mined there easily to all of the people in that northern area. Today coal is a problem for folks all through the northwest, because it costs so much money to haul it in from Edmonton over many miles, at a high rate.
The second step could be to continue the road from Meadow Lake, Saskatchewan to lac la Biche and Smith, linking up with what is known as the Northern Alberta Railway that passes through from Edmonton by way of Athabaska and Smith and on to Peace river proper.
The third step might be the extension of a line from Dawson Creek on the south side of the river, and/or from Hines Creek on the north side of the river to the coast. Whichever route is found to be more necessary and feasible could be developed first. I am not going to quarrel about that at this stage.
A fourth necessary step, it seems to me, would be a line from Grimshaw north into the Slave lake area in the Northwest Territories for bringing out the precious metals already being mined in quantity in the Yellowknife area and the district to the south.
In conclusion, let me say to the committee that I am sure the Prime Minister does not make promises lightly; and since he is retiring soon, it seems to me that he will want to make good the promises he has made already in regard to the construction of this outlet. It seems to me that he could leave no greater monument to his years of service than such an outlet from the Peace river district to the coast. The Minister of Transport, too, ought to feel that it is his responsibility to support the Prime Minister in making good his promises before his retirement. So I urge the minister to get on his fighting clothes and talk to the railroads straight from the shoulder. Let them understand that the government of the people of Canada expects them to get this job done without further delay.

Probably the hon. member would expect me to say a word in reply to his remarks. I can assure him at once that neither the government nor the Department of Transport has lost interest in the Peace river country, or in the Pacific Great Eastern and its extension into the area referred to by my hon. friend. I should like to remind him that this whole subject matter was debated at some length in 1946, I believe it was, when the hon. member for Cariboo proposed a resolution in the house. I still have in mind the committee which was set up by the premier of British Columbia. As my hon. friend knows, when

That is right.

However, I should not like the hon. gentleman to get the impression that the interest is not being shown in this great section of the country that should be shown. Since the publication of this report, the railways have been approached by the authorities of British Columbia. They have met in conference, but of course no conclusion has as yet been arrived at as to whether or not this road should be built. Many things must be taken into consideration as far as the two railways are concerned before that road can be built. I dealt with the attitude of the railways in reference to new lines. The railways have certain reservations. They feel that, unless a line can be made to pay from the standpoint of finances, some care should be taken. If it were a colonization project, then they would be more likely to ask the government for assistance.
I understand that in the far northern part of this country there are rich deposits of coal and, I am informed, of practically every other valuable mineral in the world. These are to be found in the area around Hudson Hope, Finlay Forks, Fort St. John and Slave lake. I am informed that there is vast potential wealth there, and the province of British Columbia has been giving some study to the matter, probing into the earth to make sure this wealth isj in fact, there. They go so far as to say that the coal deposits in that area are as good as, if not better than, those existing in the United States. If that be so, then I am anxious to have them brought forward. The last information I had on the subject from the British Columbia authorities was to the effect that the information would be forthcoming soon, and when it is I can assure the hon. gentleman that the project, which is important not only to his part of the country but to the whole of Canada, will be given careful consideration.

I do not think there is
much need for me to go over the whole case for the Peace river outlet, though I am glad to have this opportunity to remind the minister once more that we expect some action, and expect it very soon.
For a great many years men who have been representing both the Peace river and the Cariboo have brought this matter to the attention of parliament. On those occasions they have gone into the natural wealth of the country. They have also gone into the question of the needs of the pioneering people who went into this vast territory and proved that wealth was there. They have also shown that a railroad could be of very great service not only to the communities that have been established but to the whole of Canada.
I do not think there is anything new to be said on the question. The whole point is, what does the government intend to do about it? The minister has been very courteous and kind in his reply, as he always is, but I should like to get something a little more definite than so far he has been able to give. If the minister is listening I should like to ask to whom these recommendations he quoted were made. Who are supposed to pay attention to those five or six points?
Then I should like to know whether the minister has any information as to the intention of the government with respect to the P.G.E. and the extension of that line into the Peace river country. Has it given up its idea of building a road? Evidently it has failed in getting both the large railways of Canada to take this up as a joint project
Supply-Transport

I believe at one time it had in mind having a joint project undertaken by the provincial, and federal governments, the Canadian National, Canadian Pacific and Pacific Great Eastern-which looked like a pot-pourri to me, and very difficult to handle. Under those circumstances, no one would be responsible for building the line-or for running it afterwards, for that matter.
I do not believe that is a wise way to go at it, and I suggest that this government will have to undertake the job. I am asking that the minister go a little further. He admits that the wealth is there. He knows that already a great many people have settled there and have done a great deal of pioneering. He knows, as the hon. member for Peace River has just pointed out, that for many years these people have been paying very high freight rates, so high, in fact, as to make it almost impossible for them to carry on and make a living. He knows, too, that the opening up of that line would mean that a great many people would wish to move in from many parts of the world.
Our immigration policy is going to be stimulated; immigrants will be looking for places of settlement. There is no end of opportunity in that vast territory comprising the country referred to by the hon. member for Peace River. The minister knows all that. Added to that, he has the definite promise made by the Prime Minister, to which reference has already been made. And of course the Prime Minister is not the only one who has made those promises. From time to time all men who have been or who wanted to be prime ministers have made that promise. Seldom, however, has our present Prime Minister made a promise as definite as this one. I have read many of his promises, and there has always been some little safeguarding back door through which he could slip out, if necessary. But here is one promise to which there was no back door. It was a specific and definite promise that his government would build the line within one year. The point is that he made the unconditional promise that if it were not built by someone else it would definitely be built by his government. Also before that he made the promise, and there has been nothing to prevent his carrying it out. He said this would be done.
The Prime Minister is coming to the end of a notable political career. It would be a shame if perhaps the only promise he ever made without a back door should not be kept. I hope the minister will bring these matters to the Prime Minister's attention. If he does so, I feel sure something will be done fairly
(Mr. Irvine.]
quickly. I would ask the minister to go a little further, to give us a little more hope than he has thus far, and to tell us whether it is the intention of his department and of this government to build the line; or are they still expecting somebody else to do it?

There are two questions to which I should like to reply. The report of the committee on resources and railways, in 1945, was made to the Premier of British Columbia. The hon. member's second question was as to the intention of the government of British Columbia. I would have to direct my hon. friend to the premier of that province, if he wishes to have a statement of their intentions.
In my reply to the hon. member for Peace River I had intended to say that the government of Canada contributed substantially to the construction of the highway from Grim-shaw to Hay River in that area. I do not remember offhand w7hat the contribution was, but I believe it was more than 50 per cent.
It was 75 per cent.
The hon. member says it was 75 per cent, and I am sure he knows.

Does the minister recall that in 1946 when the debate on the Peace river outlet took place, he did suggest that the government might consider the extension of the line from Hines Creek through Hudson Hope to Finlay Forks? Has he considered the matter since that time, and would he be prepared now to commit the government to going that far at least? As I pointed out at that time, there is a large deposit of excellent coal in that area. These people are working under extraordinary difficulties to develop those natural resources. Even if he did not do any more than that, he could begin to develop that great industry up there, and in addition the line would give good service to a vast and well-settled territory.	[DOT]
There is a new opening at that point for our returned men. The Indian reserve near Fort St. John has been taken over by the department and made available for the settlement of our returned men. It would be a pity if they had to haul their supplies sixty or seventy miles even to reach a railway, let alone a market. The branch running up from Hines Creek would serve a large community and at the same time would form part of the road which some day will have to be built to the coast.

What I did say was that it might well be necessary to consider the co-ordination of highway and railway facilities, and that certain railway economists wrere of the opinion that that was the the manner in which the extension should take place. But, so far as making any specific promise-*

I was very careful on that point. I would not like to commit the government; in fact, I would have no authority to do so, without bringing it to the attention of my colleagues.
