Mr. Chairman, when the committee rose I was going to speak of the Temiscouata railway. It is an old railway built by English capital sixty odd years ago. It is the connecting link between, the Transcontinental railway and the Intercolonial railway, both now a part of the Canadian National Railways, and connecting also with the Canadian Pacific railway at Edmundston, New Brunswick. The Temiscouata railway runs from Riviere du Loup, on the south shore of the St. Lawrence river, 120 miles below Quebec, to Edmundston, New Brunswick, and then west to Connors, New Brunswick, just opposite to Fort Kent, Maine. That railway has been very active for some time, but the line needs to be reconstructed. There are great opportunities for it. In front of Edmundston, just across the Saint John river there is Madawaska, Maine, an important lumber centre. The Temiscouata railway passes through the most beautiful country in eastern Canada. Its geological formation is the same as that of the picturesque tourist country to the north of Montreal. There are three hundred lakes in my county, good hotels, and it is a paradise for tourists. The railway could help to develop the tourist trade if the necessary improvements
were made and would also help to improve trade conditions in our part of the country.
I sympathize with my hon. friends from the west and other parts of Canada when they speak on behalf of their own constituencies. That is perfectly legitimate. Canada is a young and growing country and should have the assistance of the government in these undertakings. What would have happened to the west if the Canadian Pacific had not been built some years ago with the assistance of the government? Some people complained at the time that the government was giving too much to the Canadian Pacific. But the Canadian Pacific served a national purpose in opening up a new field to Canadian endeavour. It is the same with all railways and with all steamship lines. My regret is that Canadians do not have the transportation facilities which they have a right to expect in order to visit and trade with one another. That is all the more necessary in a country of the tremendous size of Canada. Money should be spent in improving all our communications. Money spent in improving transportation facilities is always money well spent.
Hudson Bay railway, for instance.

The Hudson Bay railway has been forgotten for a time. Perhaps it was a great mistake; I am not in a position to say whether it was or not. But it was built to serve a very good purpose, and it was precisely because there was no co-operation between the steamship companies and the Canadian National Railways that the port of Churchill has not been as active as it should have been. The Hudson Bay railway is part of the great communications system of Canada. I will support the minister 100 per cent in all that he does in providing for transportation. The Temiscouata railway is one instance; the Peace River railway is another. We should see eye to eye in these matters. What difference is there between developing the Peace River railway and the Temiscouata railway. That is why I said to the hon. member for Cariboo that I was ready to support his contention, which is the same as mine, the only difference being that his railway would run through new country, while mine serves a district which has been settled for some time but in which there is some new settlement.
There are many opportunities and improvements that come with the building and maintenance of a railway. We are living in changing times; conditions now may be different from what they were some time ago. I will tell the minister what is my ambition for my part of the country, which has been forgotten
Supply-Transport

for a long time. I do not complain about the minister, but I complain to him. Last year an imposing delegation, including many mayors, came from Temiscouata to interview the minister. He received them well and gave their representations favourable consideration, but some of their recommendations have not yet been carried out.
I hope that the minister will in due course reconsider the question of maintaining and improving the Temiscouata railway so that the curves may be corrected and the line made safer. The road will then serve its purpose of being a connecting link between Maine, Mada-waska, and the St. Lawrence river. There is a fine outlet at Riviere du Loup. I appreciate the fact that the Minister of Public Works, who last year inspected the wharf at Riviere du Loup, has seen fit to have it reconstructed. It is an important piece of work that is being done there now. It is being well done. I hope that the Temiscouata railway will also be put in good shape and that we shall have an airport at Cacouna on the new route that is starting its service between Montreal and the maritimes on Thursday, May 20, of this week.
The great difficulty in far eastern Canada is that it is at too great a distance from the great centres. My district is three hundred [DOT] miles east of the city of Montreal and one hundred and twenty miles east of the city of Quebec. The ambition of everyone now is to shorten distance by adopting the easiest means of communication. We cannot expect lumber to be carried by aeroplane. It has to be carried by train and some improvements should be made in that means of transportation.
Everyone who looks to the future looks for improvements in air transport. Trans-Canada Air Lines, which comes under the minister, has done exceedingly well. Last year in the committee I did not fail to express admiration for the present Minister of Trade and Commerce who has given such an impulse to the development of the Trans-Canada Air Lines, and rightly so, because although it would have been considered unbelievable some years ago, T.C.A. is now part of our national life. Our colleagues, Mr. Chairman, realize it much better than anybody else because, owing to T.C.A., instead of spending a week to go home to the west, they can make that trip in two nights quite comfortably, and it gives them an opportunity to stay longer at home.
How is it that the businessman who is kept at his office, who cannot leave for long, can now take the plane and go anywhere in Canada within a day and come back the next day? It is because of the magnificent service

of T.C.A. It is not only for central Canada; it is not only for the western provinces, but we in eastern Canada should also have the advantage of the use of T.C.A. That is why a survey has been made of the landing facilities around Riviere du Loup, and I hope that in the near future we shall have an airport in our district. I will tell the minister how I see it. In the old days I remember English ocean liners, English steamships, weighing anchor right in front of Riviere du Loup. Some of them were loaded with lumber. Afterwards trade changed for a time and lumber has been going south to the United States. Why should we not have harbour facilities at Riviere du Loup as we had in the old times? What would be the importance of a harbour at Riviere du Loup? In the not too distant future I hope that there will be more harbour facilities. The old wharf is being rebuilt this year. In the near future we shall have a real harbour there, a harbour where ocean steamships may dock at the wharf.
We must have an airport at Riviere du Loup later, since the matter has already been considered by the Department of Transport. Coming back to what I said in the first place, I also hope that the minister will reconsider the question of improving the maintenance of the Temiscouata railway between Riviere du Loup, Edmundston, New Brunswick, and Connors, New Brunswick. If that is done I invite you, sir, and all my colleagues to come to Riviere du Loup by car, by train, by air and by sea, not by foot.

While the minister is thinking over our landing by air in Temiscouata and figuring out the answer, perhaps he will permit one of the members of the house to say a word or two with regard to the part of the country whence he comes. On Friday evening at four minutes of eleven I did not feel that I could state my case in the short time before eleven o'clock, and since then the hon. member for Temiscouata has crossed my trail. Before he gets an answer from the minister to his question of moment in the affairs of Canada, perhaps he will permit me to say a word or two with regard to what I have on my mind.
Many years ago it was a great pleasure for me to introduce to the prime minister and the members of the cabinet of that day and generation a deputation from the city of Toronto, a trainload, representing the board of trade, the harbour commissioners, the members of the city council, railway officials and what not, asking this honourable assembly to give consideration to the grade separation so necessary in the great city of Toronto. When I

Supply-Transport
looked over their plans some twenty-five years ago I found that they had asked for the separa- . tion of grade from, the Don river through to the Humber. I introduce this subject of grade separation now, Mr. Chairman, for the reason that the Minister of Transport evidently thought it might be a fit and proper place in which to say a word or two, and inasmuch as on Friday evening last in reply to the hon. member for Broadview the minister outlined what proportion of costs of grade separation and elimination of grade crossings had been given to the province of Ontario during his time as minister of that portfolio. Before he answers I immediately say through you, sir, to the minister that during the last forty years the city of Toronto has been grateful for the assistance given us in the elimination of level crossings, and for the grade separation plan, which was completed some twenty or twenty-five years ago from the Don river to the Humber. We express our appreciation to the House of Commons for that.
Those of us living in the suburban areas then felt that we were a little outside the orbit of things that were going on, but we realized that grade separation had to go on in the centre of the city. Little we thought -a quarter of a century ago how fast we would grow to the north, to the east and to the west. We could not grow fast to the south because the lake shut us off. My plea tonight, sir, is after two decades have passed, for some consideration for the areas which were then suburban but which are now part of the corporation of the city of Toronto. At that time 100,000 people lived east of the Don river; today a quarter of a million live there. We have three or four extremely dangerous level crossings in the eastern part of the city of Toronto. Unfortunately for me, I have one of them in my constituency known as Woodbine avenue level crossing. Three thousand people, vehicles and what-not cross that level crossing each, and every day. The only access children living south of that crossing have to their technical school and high school of commerce is over that particular level crossing. It is a difficult crossing to do much with. It is an expensive crossing under which to put a subway; nevertheless the powers that be, municipal and otherwise, have demanded that some consideration be given to it.
In 1912 the first order was given for some protection at that particular crossing. I remember as well as though it were yesterday in 1930 rising in my place here and before the board of railway commissioners at that time, now the board of transport commissioners, making representations on behalf of the same crossing. I remember learning many long years
ago, almost half a century ago, that the husband of a woman who was my wet nurse had been killed at that crossing fifty years ago. Tragedy after tragedy has happened on that particular crossing. It brought back to my mind a telegram, which I received, dated January 29, 1948, from the local alderman William Collings:
Serious accident Woodbine level crossing Bob Buckham seriously injured now in east general hospital. Urge pressing board of railway commissioners for okay on city's application for elimination. Will mail all correspondence city has had with commissioners and railways to date.
Alderman W. H. Collings. That is our senior alderman in the ward which I have the honour to represent in this house. I do not wish to bore the committee. This is a local matter and I rarely occupy the time of the house urging such things. There seems, however, to be no other way of bringing the matter properly before the house and putting it on the record.
On behalf of my people, I wish to say that we asked for elimination in 1912 and we got three watchmen in 1921

three watchmen on an eight-hour service. Order No. 31078 of the Board of Railway Commissioners for Canada, dated June 2, 1921, referred to the reduction of the speed limit to ten miles an hour. Trains crossing at that level were required to travel at that rate. Now, Mr. Chairman, we must be sensible, and we know that an express train cannot slow dovrn to ten miles an hour, even though there is an order to that effect.
In 1930 a subway was ordered at the same crossing, but there were, it would seem, difficulties in the way. In a letter from the late Mr. James Somers, a great public servant and clerk of the city of Toronto, whom we all honour, this gentleman, writing under date February 18, 1939, stated:
You 'will recollect correspondence which you had on the subject in 1931 and 1932 with the then mayor (Mayor Stewart).... Our files indicate that you had an appointment with the minister of railways on April 19, 1932, on this matter.
Then he states that in 1935 the late commissioner Harris discussed the matter with representatives of the Canadian National Railways and a report was submitted in 1,938 on the subject. That was in 1938, but when the war came along in 1939 the matter was again shelved, and the city council approved the request made to the federal authorities to eliminate this level crossing. The application was not pressed, however, because we were too much war-minded in 1939 to think about level crossings. Therefore, owing to the intervention of the second great war, the application was not proceeded with.

Formal application was made by the city solicitor on November 25, 1947, to the board of transport commissioners for an order to direct the Canadian National Railways to construct a subway at Woodbine avenue and apportion the costs. The city's application reads in part:
Woodbine avenue is a public highway running north and south in the eastern section of the city of Toronto and is a thoroughfare that carries a very great vehicular traffic that is continually increasing. The level crossing at Woodbine avenue is now protected by gates which greatly impede the movement of traffic.
The city solicitor has been furnished' with a copy of the letter dated December 22, 1947, addressed 'to the secretary of the board of transport commissioners by the assistant general solicitor for the Canadian National Railways.
Through you, Mr. Chairman, I wish to impress upon the .minister the fact that there is a tremendous amount of traffic in that area, east and west, north and south, embracing a population of a quarter of a million people. We in our community feel disposed to press this matter until it is brought to a satisfactory conclusion. As long ago as 1918, which is thirty years ago, it was my high privilege to be president of the Danforth businessmen's association and we asked for action. The war was barely over and times were difficult, but we made representations until the second great war broke out, and then we sat aside because we had that great tragic event facing us. Now, however, we are disposed to press for this particular grade crossing elimination.
We have been fair all through the picture for three decades, but as a member of this house I do not intend to sit idly by, even if there is a shortage of steel for work of this kind. I do not purpose to listen to the plaint of even the Minister of Trade and Commerce, now charged with the responsibility of conserving Canadian dollars in connection with steel requirements. I do not purpose to wait any longer. On behalf of a quarter of a million people who use this particular subway, I am going to ask consideration from this honourable assembly.
I do not intend to sit quietly by, much as I admire the manner in which the Minister of Transport conducts his department, and listen to statements that Ontario has had more than its fair share of crossing eliminations or more than its fair share of treatment from the railways. It is quite true, as the minister said on Friday last, that the central region of the Canadian National Railways has done such and so, but two sentences he
used should have been coupled together. He should have said that the central region receives a great deal of traffic from that same area. I am glad he made that statement, for it moderates the first half of his sentence.
Let me say to the minister, through you, Mr. Chairman: Do not divide us up into sections in Canada when it comes to expenditures. I ask the minister through you, Mr. Chairman, to chastize any member from the central region of Ontario or the city of Toronto who complains at any time about any expenditure for fisheries, any expenditure in connection with the salmon fisheries of British Columbia, or any expenditure under an appropriation of $41,672,000 for agriculture, because we have not a farm within the community which I am now discussing.
I have not objected to any of the expenditures that I have indicated, and I am thinking of the other members of this committee who tonight will rise in their places and vote half a million dollars to eliminate a crossing which constitutes a hazard to a quarter of a million people.
Have I, sir, at any time ever refused appropriations for dried-out areas or for flooded districts in western Canada? No. We are all a part of the whole. Have I at any time refused anything to the Pacific salmon industry, of which I admit I do not know very much? Have I refused any assistance to the miners for whom the hon. member for Cape Breton South pleads? Let us be men, men of bigger calibre than that. And so I make this request on behalf of a quarter of a million people. I say to the minister: Now that we are in committee, do not put me in the awkward position of having to rise again and assure the house that the amount of money needed for this level crossing elimination must be expended. I am asking the minister to pay attention to what I say and, in reply, not to refuse me. I am asking him to think in broad terms, and of the millions we voted for many other parts of Canada, without let or hindrance. I sometimes wonder why, but more often say it was to carry on Canada as one great country and not one little part of the central region of the Canadian National Railways.

Before I deal with the request made by the hon. member for Danforth, perhaps I might be allowed to say a word in connection with the Temiscouata railway matter which was raised by the hon. member for Temiscouata. As the hon. gentleman said, the Temiscouata railway is one which has been operating under difficult circumstances. For-

Supply-Transport
tunately it is managed by a man who has had a great deal of experience and who deserves a tremendous amount of commendation for the way in which he has operated the railway under the circumstances I mentioned a moment ago.
The railway connects the town of Riviere du Loup with Edmundston, and then goes on to a place called Connors. Because of the difficulties in which it found itself, and as a result of representations which were made to the department last year, I set up a committee to study the various points which were brought to the attention of the department. I think that committee did excellent work because, as a result of it, while it came to the conclusion that it would not be profitable from the standpoint of the Canadian National Railways at least to purchase the railway, it was still felt that the railway had been doing such excellent work that some assistance should be given to it. Because of the recommendations made by the committee not only was it found possible to increase the wages of certain of the employees who had been working under difficult circumstances, but it was also provided that a greater amount of revenue would be given to the Temiscouata railway from both the Canadian National and the Canadian Pacific railways. Free rental of equipment was also provided. While it was not possible to grant all the requests which were made by the delegation that called on the department, I still think a step in the right direction was taken. I can assure the hon. gentleman that his remarks will be considered' and brought to the attention of those who are responsible for giving additional traffic to the Temicouata railway.
The hon. member for Danforth dealt with the crossing at Woodbine. Let me say to him immediately, having regard to his reference to what I had to say on Friday evening, that it was far from my mind to attempt to show that one province was receiving from the grade crossing fund far more than another. I was simply replying to his colleague, the hon. member for Broadview, who made the statement that the province of Ontario received little-in fact, at one stage he said it received practically nothing-from the Department of Transport. I attempted to reply to that. I am glad the hon. member for Danforth agrees with me in the statement which I made.
He dealt with a difficult position which existed at Woodbine. Not only does that position exist there, but there are five other level crossings in the city of Toronto which deserve careful attention. The application with regard to the Woodbine improvement is now before the board of transport commissioners. As the
hon. gentleman knows, before a project can be approved, representations must be heard from those who make the application, from the railways which are interested in it and which also, in due course, will be required to pay a substantial amount of the cost of the project if it is approved. Evidence must also be given by the engineers who give consideration to the project. My hon. friend should know that the board of transport commissioners cannot grant the request for that railway crossing without a hearing, and without giving the application the attention it deserves.
The application is filed, of course.

Yes; it is now before the board of transport commissioners. If it is approved, then a substantial sum of money- 40 per cent of the cost, not in any event to exceed $100,000-will be paid out of the grade crossing fund. I presume that the remainder of the cost will be divided, in accordance with the usual custom, between the railways and the municipality concerned. My hon. friend will be pleased to know that the board of transport commissioners is proceeding to the city of Toronto early next month to hear the representations in connection with the project. I hope my hon. friend will obtain his request.
If I might make an interpolation here, may I say that they have been there and have made a survey of this particular project.
They are now proceeding to have a formal hearing and listen to representations, after which they will make a decision.
I thank the minister for what he said a moment ago.

I want to take a few minutes to ask for the minister's consideration of something pertaining to my constituency and also to all the southern part of Manitoba. As no doubt the minister is well aware, discussions have taken place in the west regarding the extension of the Gypsumville line, up through Grand Rapids to Wekusko which is mile 81 on the Hudson Bay railway.
What is the name of the railway, please? I am sorry that I did not catch it.

The Canadian National, from Gypsumville right up through Grand Rapids to mile 81 on the Hudson Bay railway. Building these 190 miles of railroad would mean a saving of 250 rail miles on the route to Port Churchill. The extension needed would be 190 miles of new railroad. From a military
Supply-Transport

defence viewpoint, as well as providing a great commercial saving, this interlake cut-off should receive serious and favourable consideration. It would also open up that country which is practically undeveloped. It is a good timber country and is in many places good agricultural country. It would be a good place for settlers if there were a railroad through it. I feel quite sure that- the Manitoba government would support such an extension, although I have never discussed this matter with any responsible minister of that government. I hope to do so, however, at the first opportunity I have.
I should like the Minister of National Defence to give this extension serious consideration also, from a national defence point of view, and how it would save 250 miles of rail distance between Winnipeg and the port of Churchill. With a shorter haul to Churchill, it will put the port in a much more favourable position for the shipment of live cattle to Britain. With the. elimination of this 250 mile haul, it would eliminate practically two divisions in the railroad. Many savings could be made on different kinds of freight. In this connection, livestock could be shipped more cheaply. There would be a shorter haul and there would be less expense, as the cattle would be eighteen to twenty hours less on the road and would be unloaded fewer times for water and feed. Food products going to the port by refrigerator oars would make a saving also, as they would not have to be re-iced as often as on the longer hauls. All general merchandise for export manufactured in and around Winnipeg would benefit from this short cut to the port of Churchill. Winnipeg is growing in population and developing in industry, and is looking for her own seaport for an outlet to the markets of the world.
The argument has been put forward that the port of Churchill is open for only ninety-eight days in the year. Even if that is so, we should take advantage of that time, and with the modern devices now available no doubt that period could be extended.
I do not want to take up too much time on this matter, but wish only to ask the minister's consideration. I want him to look into it and really consider it. It looks good to me, and this short cut to Churchill certainly would be to the benefit of Manitoba as a whole. I could make quite a long speech on this subject, but I do not want to do that at this time; I only want to bring the matter to the attention of the minister so that he and his officers may look into it. I should like to read the resolution passed at the annual con-

vention of the Hudson bay route association held at Regina, Saskatchewan, on March 17, 1948:
Resolution:	Hudson Bay railway short cut
off to Winnipeg through inter-lake region in Manitoba.
Whereas it is considered to be in the best interest of the Hudson bay route and southern Manitoba and centra] United States points to shorten the present rail mileage between Port Churchill and the city of Winnipeg by a reduction of the present distance by about 225 miles through the construction of a short rail link of some 190 miles known as Manitoba inter-lake region out-off located between lake Winnipeg on the east and lake Manitoba, lake Dauphin and lake Winnipegosis on the west and commencing at Wekusko, mile 81, on the Hudson Bay railway, to connect with the present C.N.R. rail terminus at Gypsumville, Manitoba.
Therefore be it resolved that this association do hereby urge upon the dominion government and the C.N.R. the immediate necessity of constructing this short rail link between Weku-sko on the Hudson Bay railway and Gypsumville on the 'Canadian National Railway at the earliest possible date.
I cannot add anything to this resolution, other than to ask the minister's serious consideration.
I shall be glad to bring the matter to the attention of the officers of the Canadian National Railways.

Again this evening I should like to bring to the attention of the minister the matter of the Bodo and Airways branch line. This question has been dealt with in detail on many other occasions by the hon. member for Acadia and myself, and for that reason I do not intend to go into it in detail tonight. As hon. members are well aware, some years ago the grade was constructed, and is still standing there. This line runs through an agricultural district, and production could be greatly increased if the steel were laid on that grade. I am sure the minister has had many representations to this effect from boards of trade and farmer organizations in that district, and I hope something may be done in the very near future to complete this line. As it is now, freight and passengers are hauled out to a certain point to the east, and again to another point to the west, but in between they have to get along as best they can.
In the northern part of my territory are two other lines, Heinsburg-Frenchman's Butte and the Bonnyville line, about which I have no doubt the hon. member for The Battlefords and the hon. member for North Battleford will speak. Having joined with them on other occasions, however, I should like again to impress upon the minister the importance of

completing those two lines of rail for the development of what may be called this north country and for the greater production of agricultural commodities which are badly needed at the present time.

I have a matter I should like to bring to the attention of the minister, about which he probably knows something, though I am not sure of what either he or his department can do about it. I am referring to the smoke nuisance in the city of Toronto and in other cities as well.
I do not know whether the minister realizes the quantity of smoke that may be seen at the entrance to Toronto but I should like to know if there is anything that can be done about it. Not long ago I got off the train in Toronto and walked from the union station over toward Bay street in order to get a car. A short time before there had been a fresh fall of snow, but the snow was no longer white; it was black. This smoke question is a serious matter as far as the health of the citizens of Toronto is concerned. When you come there either from the east or the west you see a pall of smoke hanging over the railway yards. If you come in from the northwest you also encounter this smoke in the vicinity of the railway yards. I know it is not altogether the fault of the railways. The city has its inspectors going around trying to control the amount of smoke in the air, but to my mind very little has been done by the railways along that line.
I do not know what can be done about it, but the situation is serious and is getting more serious all the time. With the growth of the city, the growth of the yards, and the amount of traffic moving, this matter is becoming a real problem. When you approach from the south you can notice the smoke hanging over the city, and the situation is becoming worse in northwest and northeast Toronto. So I was wondering if the department was doing anything to abate that nuisance.
Of course in a city like Toronto the answer is to electrify these railways, but that would be a tremendous expense right now. However, it seems to me something could be done about the matter. Perhaps the minister has something in mind; perhaps the board of transport commissioners have something to suggest. I know the railways have been warned by the city that they must obey the smoke bylaw, but as you know it is impossible for the railways to do as a factory would do in this connection.
This is something that cannot go on, and be neglected, because this smoke nuisance has a serious effect. The other day I noticed in the newspapers that smoke is suspected of
having some bearing on cancer of the lungs, and certainly it has a great deal to do with bronchial diseases of one kind and another. The health of our citizens must be considered, and I am bringing this matter to the attention of the minister, so that he may tell me whether anything is being done to correct the situation.

The hon. member has raised a question which, I am sure, is of extreme importance to the citizens of Toronto and those of all other large centres affected by railway traffic, and I want to thank him for the very moderate way in which he has dealt with the matter. The complete answer, of course, is electrification of the railways, but that is a matter of extreme cost. Each year, however, the railways-and I refer now particularly to the Canadian National, though I know this applies to some extent to the Canadian Pacific as well-are spending considerable sums of money on new equipment. No doubt the hon. gentleman is acquainted with the fact that a trial run was made from Toronto to Montreal with diesel equipment, and it is the intention to add to the present number of diesels as time goes on. That will not meet the problem immediately, nor will it meet the problem completely. So that in view of the serious position which exists there, I have asked the board of transport commissioners to set up a committee to deal with the problem of smoke nuisance in congested areas. This was done about two months ago.
What will come out of it I do not know. They are giving consideration to a new mechanical device which can 'be applied to roundhouses, thereby eliminating in part the smoke coming from those round-houses. Again in Toronto the Canadian Pacific Railway Company have what is known as pre-steaming. It does not eliminate the smoke altogether, but it does a great deal toward lessening the nuisance.
I can assure the hon. member that the Department of Transport is wide awake to this extremely acute and important problem; and the committee which has been given the power to study and make a report will, I hope, bring in something of a satisfactory nature.
I thank the minister for saying that I was moderate in my demands. I must say I do not feel moderate when I speak about this matter, because it is a very serious one.

I support the representations made by the hon. member for Selkirk in connection with the construction of a railway from Gypsumville, Manitoba, to Wekusko on the Hudson Bay railway. I do not intend to make further comments on that matter. I think it should be said, however, that before the war a trial shipment of cattle was made from Churchill to Great Britain. The British importers reported that those cattle reached British ports in better condition than similar shipments from maritime ports. I suggest that is some proof that use could be made of the route in the future in connection with the shipment of cattle.
I should like to point out one further fact in connection with trade through Churchill in the near future. The Hudson bay route association has done a great deal toward advocating trade between western Canada and Great Britain through the Churchill route. This association has recently investigated the possibility of importing British coal from Wales. The last information I received on the subject was to the effect that British coal could be landed at Churchill for $19.65 a ton. The shipping rate from Churchill to Le Pas is approximately twenty cents per 100 pounds, or $4 a ton. I should like to know if it would be possible to get the carload rate from Churchill to Le Pas, since the coal being brought in in ship would be arriving in large quantities and undoubtedly would move out of Churchill by trainload. It might therefore be possible to get a flat rate from* Churchill to Le Pas which would fall somewhat short of the present rate of twenty cents per 100 pounds.
I would ask the minister to investigate the possibility of developing this trade on a twoway basis, since we would be shipping grain and other products to Great Britain.
Another matter which should be considered in connection with the development of the coal trade would be the possibility of importing coal to western Canada from* the maritime provinces, particularly from the Sydney area. I understand that there are fourteen large coal mines on Cape Breton island, and it ought to be possible to develop the coal trade between Nova Scotia and western Canada by way of the Churchill route.
It is quite true, of course, that there would be some point in central Manitoba and Saskatchewan where coal from Alberta could compete ; and south of that, shipments from eastern Canada, because of the transportation costs, would not be economically sound.
I have already dealt with the possibility of developing the grain trade with the maritime provinces in connection with the building up

of the livestock industry. That was in another debate, and I do not intend to cover it again this evening.
One other point about which the people in Churchill particularly, and those in northern Manitoba and northern Saskatchewan, are concerned is the possibility of extending the shipping season over the Hudson bay route. At the present time it is stated that ships can go in and out of Churchill for ten weeks a year. Of course that is a very short shipping season. However, there are a great many people, particularly those living in Churchill, who believe that the season could be extended. Only recently the Minister of National Defence announced that the Royal Canadian Navy is to hold its exercises this summer in Hudson bay. I would ask the two ministers-the Minister of Transport and the Minister of National Defence-to get together in the matter and, while the navy is exercising in those northern waters, they might investigate the possibility of extending the shipping season to four or five or even six months.
It might also be necessary, if the coal trade is to be developed through Churchill to the western provinces, to have facilities built at the docks in Churchill for the unloading of coal, so as to facilitate handling.

I wish to take only a few moments of the time of the committee to bring up a transportation matter of great importance to the people of the maritime provinces. This matter has been before the House of Commons on numerous occasions. As a matter of fact, I suppose it is one of the oldest transportation problems in Canada.

That sounds like
Chignecto.

Yes, I refer to the Chignecto canal. The minister has anticipated me in this, and I am pleased indeed to know that he has this important matter on his mind.
I have said thait this is an old subject. As a matter of fact, it goes back to the days of French rule in Acadia. In 1686 it was recommended by the then governor of Acadia to the King of France. I might say it has been investigated and surveyed many times since, but, unfortunately, as yet nothing has been done. The province of New Brunswick even before confederation had the site surveyed, and it was only because of a lack of funds at that time that the project was not proceeded with.
In 1871 Sir John A. Macdonald felt eo keenly in the matter that he promised the people of the maritime provinces that the Chignecto canal would be built. Unfortun-

Supply-Transport
ately, shortly after this Sir John was defeated, and Sir Alexander Mackenzie, who became Prime Minister, found the economic conditions of the dominion in bad shape, with the result that he shelved the project for the time being.
In connection with the attitude of Sir John A. Macdonald, I should like to quote what was said by Sir Hugh Allan, chairman of a commission appointed by Sir John at that time. This will give hon. members some idea of the importance in which the building of this canal was held by the leading politicians and statesmen of that day. Sir Hugh Allan, reporting to Sir John A. Macdonald, had this to say:
Inseparably connected with the growth of intercolonial trade is the construction of the Baie Verte canal across the isthmus of Chig-necto connecting the provinces of Nova Scotia and New Brunswick. The advantages that must accrue not only to the commerce of the maritime provinces, but to the dominion as a whole, are so clearly pointed out by the boards of trade of all the leading cities of Canada and by men interested in the development of our commercial interests, not simply by the merchants of Saint John and other places in the locality of the proposed canal but merchants of Toronto, Hamilton, Ottawa, Montreal and Quebec, that it is superfluous for the commissioners to do more than briefly refer to a few salient features of the scheme.
Then Sir Hugh Allan goes on to point out, as he states, the salient features of the scheme. The ohief feature was that it would reduce by over 400 miles transportation from Montreal, Quebec and the head of the lakes to Saint John and ports on the Atlantic in the United States.
I am satisfied that if this canal had been built, as it should have been built, in those early days in the history of this country it would have paid for itself many times over and would have greatly developed that section of the Dominion of Canada. I shall not go into its many advantages tonight because the subject has been often debated in the house and I have taken part in the discussions on numerous occasions. But it is still a very live issue in the maritime provinces. I would point out to the minister that practically every board of trade in the maritime provinces has recommended the construction of the Chignecto canal. The leading newspapers of that section have been demanding it now for the past two or three years, particularly the Telegraph-Journal of the city of Saint John.
I would also call the attention of the minister and of the committee to the fact that the people of the maritimes have never complained of expenditures in other parts of the country. We have heard a lot this evening,
for instance, of the Hudson Bay railway. I am satisfied that the Chignecto canal would have been of far more benefit to this country and the maritime provinces than the Hudson Bay railway. However, we in the maritime provinces never complained about the amount of money that we had to contribute to the building of the Hudson Bay railway, nor have we complained about the many millions of dollars which our section of the country has had to pay as its share for the building of canals in every other part of Canada.
Looking over the history of canals in this country, I find that Sir John A. Macdonald in his day listed the canal projects of Canada under these heads: first, those that were imperative to the economic development of this country. One of the canals which headed that list was the Chignecto canal between Nova Scotia and New Brunswick. I would also point out that every canal on that list, and there were many of them, has been built except the Chignecto canal. Under the second head he listed canals which were highly desirable for the development of this country. All those, too, have been built, and we in our part of the country have contributed our share to their building and maintenance. But still the Chignecto canal, which is as important today as it was then, remains unbuilt. Many of these other canals on which millions of dollars have been spent are today overgrown with weeds and are nothing but a liability to the dominion.
In conclusion, I hope that the minister will give this matter, which is of great importance to us, his most serious consideration, and that it will receive from this government or whatever other government may be in power the attention which it rightly deserves.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to support the remarks of my seatmate, the hon. member for Royal, with respect to the Chignecto canal. It is a project that has been before the people of this country since the days of the Acadians, three hundred and more years ago. The route was even used by the Indians in portaging across that part of Nova Scotia. The Chignecto canal was projected before confederation by the maritime provinces at an estimated cost of $8,000,000, and I am just as satisfied as that I am standing here that if the maritime provinces had not entered into confederation-I am not saying that I have ever been or am now opposed to that step-the three maritime provinces would, as a matter of commercial necessity, have built that canal long ago, and we would not have had to wait until this day and plead session after session, as I and many

others have done, for justice from this government with respect to the construction of that canal.
There has been expended in Canada for canals-I gave these figures last year-a total of $243,752,399.78. There has been paid for deficits on the canals, $114,130,209.81, or a total of $357,882,609.59. Hardly a dollar of that has been expended in the maritime provinces. Possibly a little has been spent for maintenance of the St. Peter's canal, which was built before confederation, and another small canal for small fishing vessels.
We have contributed toward the capital cost and toward the deficits of the canals in central Canada; these canals with their lake and river services give cheap transportation, and the railways meet such freight rates. We in the maritime provinces have contributed our share to enable them to be constructed and maintained, but we do not get this cheap transportation.
In the estimates this year I find, for the maintenance of canals, the sum of $3,886,408, and last year there was expended for that purpose $3,830,580. In addition, there is a large expenditure of several million dollars for capital account in dredging ship channels in central Canada and in improving their canals and waterways. We have no like expenditure in our part of Canada.
It has been pointed out that the Chignecto canal was approved by the Prime Minister of this country, Sir John A. Macdonald, in 1871. A charter was granted in 1882 to construct a ship railway. Engineers approved the ship railway rather than the canal, and there was spent by private enterprise on that project $4,000,000 or more. This company organized by British capital, asked for an extension of its charter for two or three years because the failure of its banking firm, Baring Brothers, left it unable to proceed with the work as contemplated. They estimated it would take $1,500,000 to complete the project, but the extension of their charter was not granted, and we did not get the ship railway or the canal. The federal government had authorized a subsidy of $150,000 for a term of twenty-five years which was later changed to $170,000 for twenty years. But all that was cancelled and not a dollar was spent by the federal government toward the construction of the canal or the ship railway. If the amount promised at that time by way of subsidy, on the strength of which private capital invested their money in the project, was capitalized at compound interest I venture to say it would amount today to $15,000,000, and that sum is certainly due us

in our part of Canada along with any additional amounts necessary to complete that work.
A survey was made in 1930 to 1932, and an estimate W'as made of $23,000,000 for the smaller canal and $35,000,000 for the larger canal. Engineers felt that these estimates were swollen. We have been told that the canal will not pay at this cost. Such a canal should not be required to pay. Certainly the canals in central Canada have not paid. It is a commercial necessity; it is a defence measure, but it is the only project of its kind that I know of which has been placed upon a basis of whether or not it will pay.
As pointed out by the previous speaker, boards of trade in the maritime provinces, mayors, and members of provincial legislatures have sponsored the construction of the Chignecto canal. People in the Annapolis valley, fruit growers and their boards of trade have asked for the construction of the canal. They require, more than ever before, easy access to the markets of central Canada for their fruit. They feel that, especially with the increased freight rates, they should have this canal and should get the benefit of any reduction in freight that can be made available to them. The production of coal, gypsum, lumber and other products in the maritime provinces would benefit. The people of Prince Edward Island require it for the shipment of their produce to the United States and the south.
A transportation commission and committees have been organized to press our needs and claims. We are not satisfied with promises, with being put off. Perhaps it is because we do not speak with a united voice in the maritime provinces that we do not get action.
Notwithstanding our freight difficulties, there has been established, within the last few weeks, in the town of Amherst, a branch of ihe American "Bendix Industry", which is a pleasing departure from what has occurred in the past in the maritimes. That is the first large industry, I believe, that has ever attempted to establish a branch in the maritime provinces. It will manufacture household utensils, such as washing machines. It will soon employ 200 men and, I hope, expand. I want to express my appreciation to the Minister of Trade and Commerce, the government of Nova Scotia, the board of trade, the Canadian Manufacturers' Association and the individuals who have contributed toward the introduction of that industry in the maritime provinces, thereby changing the whole past
