trend of industry in Canada. I hope it will be the forerunner of many such industries.

I wish at this time to express my thanks, and also the thanks of the Port Alberni harbour commissioners, to the minister and to his able staff for the courteous consideration which we have received from them during the past year. In the remarks I intend to make tonight, I shall try to be helpful and constructive. I wish first to deal with the matter of a coastguard service for Canada. I know this matter has been brought up on several occasions. I am thinking particularly of the question asked on February 9 last by the hon. member for Skeena and of what the minister said at that time. I can understand: why he felt that way, that this new coastguard service would be quite costly. Probably he felt that the estimates of the Department of Transport could not be stretched to that limit. He then went on to enumerate the services that were provided to protect our sailors on the coast. While I am not at all familiar with what is on the Atlantic coast in the way of equipment, I can say to him that I have had an intimate association with both the lifesaving services and the aids to navigation service of his department for the past twenty-five years on the British Columbia coast. I may say to him that he has been able to obtain excellent men to staff his agency. I can also assure him that the crews, coxswains and officers of his lifesaving vessels are able and capable men.
As I say, I am very familiar with the equipment that he has on the coast. I do not think it has ever been the minister's privilege to look at the lifesaving equipment that his department maintains. I am quite sure that if he had a look at it, even a layman like himself-I am sure he is not a sailor-would get some appreciation of the sense of futility which must be in the minds of the men who are working in this service. The lifesaving equipment which we have on the Pacific coast which, I may say, is one the great world trade routes, and well known as the graveyard of the Pacific, consists of two 40-foot boats; I am guessing at that now. I think the minister will find that nearly right. They are practically open boats. I am quite sure that if the crew ever had to go out into one of these northern Pacific gales in the middle of winter the crew would perish probably long before they could give any help. They would be in much greater danger than anybody who happened, to be out there in a vessel merely in distress.
As far as the boats are concerned, I said that they were forty feet long and practically open. There is only a canvas cover in front
of them that the crew can huddle underneath. There is a small cockpit over the engine that will hold the engineer in case of emergency. I would imagine that he would suffocate if he had to stay in there more than about fifteen minutes. If anyone gets into difficulty on the Pacific coast he must, of course, depend on the United States coastguard service for any help. I am sure the minister will realize that the boats *we have there equipped neither with radio telephone nor radar are entirely inadequate for the service they are intended to perform. If a ship gets into difficulty out there in the wintertime, or at any other time with poor visibility, there is no possibility of one of our boats locating that ship in the tens of thousands of square miles of Pacific ocean, without the use of radar and some of the modern navigation equipment that is now available.
I quite agree that a coastguard is costly. It has always seemed to me that a coastguard is a service that should be organized and maintained by the Department of National Defence. I understand that is the way in which the United States coastguard operates. It operates as a unit of the national defence service there.
The matter of cost has been brought up many times. I think Canada has reached a stage in the world now that we should be able to offer an adequate coastguard service, if we are to be a maritime nation. We are starting to have great ideas about what our maritime commission will do. I see by the papers that we intend to subsidize the construction of fast freighters and we intend to be a sea-going nation.
As regards the matter of costs, it has always seemed to me that our governments are not as efficient in getting value for their dollars as private industry is. If the minister recalls, not long ago War Assets of Canada were disposing of a large number of vessels. We had the Bangor type of diesel mine-sweepers which sold at the low price of one-tenth of cost. They would be suitable vessels for this work. I believe the thirty or forty Fairmiles, sold on the east coast and the west coast at $3,000 apiece, could have been converted to diesel power at about $10,000, and I make that statement advisedly. They would have made excellent ships. I would point out that the United States war assets corporation had what they call the Y type mine-sweepers, a 135-foot vessel powered with a 1,200 horsepower diesel engine, equipped with direction finders, echo sounders, radar and every modem navigation device, and they sold these vessels, even throwing in a Bendix washing machine, for $15,000. A good many Canadian fishing companies purchased them.
Supply-Transport

It seemed to me most unfortunate that, at this cost, when the vessels were available to us, and considering the serviceable boats they would have made for coastguard use, advantage was not taken of that opportunity. I think it is important for the minister to discuss the matter with the Minister of National Defence.
We all know that as soon as we get into international difficulties we usually have to turn 'to the commercial fishermen and commercial sailors to augment our navy in time of emergency, and I can think of no better way to train men than to have them as part of national defence for coastguard service. On the Pacific coast four of these vessels could be stationed at strategic points in communication with one another by radio telephone and in communication with the lighthouses located along the coast.
Let me make this plea with the minister. I as a 'Canadian, and I am sure he feels the same way, have been terribly ashamed at times at the fact that whenever a Canadian vessel got into trouble the only vessel available on the Pacific coast, capable of towing anything into port, was a United States coastguard boat.
Just before I conclude, I wish to bring to the attention of the minister another matter. It has to do with direction finding stations. I am sure the minister has received a brief from the fishermen's co-operative association, dated February 9 last. It was a resolution setting out the necessity for more adequate direction finding stations there. I see by a perusal of the estimates that there appears to be another $174,000 grant in this particular branch of the service this year, and I trust that this sum of money indicates that the minister will find it possible to provide these extra facilities which are so badly needed on the Pacific coast.

In reply to the hon. member for Comox-Alberni, I wish I could give more satisfaction than I did when I replied to a question asked on February 9 by an hon. member, but unfortunately the position as it was then has not changed. However, in view of his interest and that of other hon. members, I shall be glad to review the situation again.
I do not wish to go into the reasons I gave then, but my hon. friend will be interested to know that there is provided in the estimate something for lifesaving equipment in the way of a new lifeboat at Bamfield, British Columbia, which will cost $55,000 or $56,000. That does not come near the point my hon. friend has raised as to providing coastguard service on both coasts. That is a question which is so far-reaching that it must be considered not

by one department but by other departments of government as well. In view of his representations I shall be glad to consider the matter with my colleagues.

I wish to call the minister's attention to two or three matters and I can assure him that I do not intend to prolong this discussion, because there are many others who wish to take part. I took part in the discussion on Friday night. I may say that I have known the minister for a great many years, longer in fact than I have known some of the members of the government, and I think he has been quite courteous and most attentive to his duties. I will not say anything further tonight than to refer to a few subjects dealt with.
The other night I was referring to the present estimates of the Department of Transport, and with it the department of the Minister of Public Works in reference to our city. I referred to the question of grade crossings.
The minister must not forget that the city of Toronto paid one-third of the total cost of the Toronto viaduct along the waterfront. That city has contributed more taxes than any other city in the dominion. I am not here to argue tonight that we should undertake vast public expenditures at a time when we are faced with a housing situation, high building costs and all the rest of it. I would refer the minister, however, to the returns I received from his department with reference to the grade crossing fund. I had asked a question as to what sums of money had been spent on grade crossings during 1947, and the answer was that there were no contributions to the grade crossing fund in the city of Toronto during that year.
It is true they did have one grade crossing in the northwest grade separation, and it is true that the public works department has done some work in connection with the post office in Toronto, nearly all a revote. But I would point out that such work was absolutely necessary, in view of the fact that a revenue of $15,500,000 is derived from the post office in that city.
The other night I referred to a steam suburban service, something we have never had in our lives in our district, and we have not been able to get it, no matter what government was in. Why, I do not know.
There was another matter I wanted to bring to the attention of the minister. The minister refers to the Canadian National Rail-

Supply-Transport
ways and their estimates. I am not a member of the committee on railways and shipping which is revising those estimates, but I suggest that you will go a long way 'before you will find another city doing what our city did in connection with the Toronto viaduct in the central region of the Canadian National Railways, which accounts for a large part of the revenue-producing section of the province, the Niagara district and the Toronto district, extending right across the central part of the province where most of the revenue comes from.
We have hoped for a car ferry from Toronto to Port Dalhousie and a new boat on lake Ontario there, in the place of the Northumberland, just as we have been hoping for a steam suburban service in return for the large expenditures the city has made. I would ask the minister, before the session concludes, to make a statement on the present position of the St. Lawrence waterway and navigation.
That is a tough one.

The minister smiles. May I remind him that he has already appointed another waterway commission-to do what, I do not know-in connection with the Lachine section. One of these gentlemen is Mr. Henry, who was one of the pioneers in the Beauhar-nois matter about which we heard something years ago.
He is Canada's greatest economist.

The minister was then going to law school, and we heard enough about Beauharnois for years. May I point out to the minister that the returns he tabled for me some time ago to which I referred, in connection with grade crossings, speak for themselves.
I was referring to the estimates of the Minister of Public Works, who I hope will come up and visit Toronto harbour some day, because we would like to see him up there. I suggest May 22. I think that would be a nice day for him to come up. That is next Saturday. If he cannot come then, I hope he comes some other day.
Having made these few remarks, that is all I have to say. I know the hon. member for Lincoln is anxious to say something. In conclusion, may I say that we do not want anything to which we are not entitled. We get little from any government anyway.

While we are discussing the matter of grade crossings tonight, Mr. Chairman, I wish to draw the attention of the
minister, through you, to a condition existing just outside the city of Belleville. The Canadian National yards have been growing and extending. In my lifetime the roadway crossing from the south side to the north side has been twice moved in an easterly direction. Today it is getting down to a point where it cannot be moved again, because the coal chutes and the water tank are just a little bit to the east of it. There is a crossing there which is used, not by a quarter of a million of people, the number mentioned by the hon. member for Danforth, but by a large number of people because it is still a suburban area, and just to the east of it is a good agricultural country, from which comes into the city a good deal of traffic. There are five or six tracks there at the present time, and it is looked upon as a dangerous condition. I believe the municipalities and the suburban road commission have been making some representations. That is my understanding, anyway. I hope the minister or the appropriate authorities will take this matter into consideration. I know from personal experience what it is like to go across there on a windy night in the winter, with the steam from the locomotives blowing down on you. You do not know where you are. There is not even a guard at that crossing. This is a condition that deserves some consideration at the hands of the department.

I want to remind the minister of a few things. This evening lie has been asked to build a number of railroads and one or two other things. I thought, while he had his pick and shovel in his hands and his track layer out, he might as well finish up a few little jobs that need to be done out our way.
I want to remind him of the stretch of road between Neidpath and Swift Current. This is not a difficult road to finsh. The Canadian National runs from Radville up through that country. Passengers coming up to Swift Current can get within twenty miles of there, and then they must get some other means of travel. It does not seem reasonable that people can come within that distance of the largest trading centre in that part of Saskatchewan and not be able to finish the rest of their trip.
There is a considerable amount of fairly heavy traffic in there which the railroad could use. The roadbed is built in most places. It may be run down a bit, but I think it is built, if not completely all the way through, very nearly so. The steel is laid six miles farther west than Neidpath as far as Burnham. The job is not one that would be called a difficult one, nor would it be an expensive undertaking.
Supply-Transport

If it pays to bring stuff up to Neidpath and take it back out, obviously the other twenty miles would pay its own way in operation.
I should like the minister to tell me whether he has given any consideration to this since I first mentioned it in 1945, and again in 1940 and in 1947; I suppose I can do so again in 1949 if he has forgotten about it till now.
Another thing to which I should like some consideration given is the completion of a line that runs from Pennant down to Verio where the end of steel now is. At one time it was contemplated it would continue on to join with a branch line that connects with Fox Valley about fifty miles straight west of Verio. At one time it was intended also to bring the line from Golden Prairie, which is also at the end of the line, up to meet that and so give a network of railroad service right through that country where there is a large amount of wheat, some large cattle ranches, sheep ranches, fur farms and so on that could be served. If the minister has not given consideration to this as a result of my past representations, I wish he would take note of it; and if he has, I should like him to tell me the result of his consideration up to date.

I am glad to tell the hon. gentleman that I asked the railways to give consideration, not only to his representations which were made heretofore but to those of other hon. members who have from time to time and from year to year made observations with reference to branch lines or new construction. The railways-and when I use that term in the plural, I mean the Canadian National Railways-have given consideration to those projects. In fact, they have set up a committee to study them, and they have come to the conclusion that all these branch lines at the moment should be divided into two classes: first, that which the railway feels it should recommend on the basis of improving or rounding out its system and serving territories now without service and which lines can be economically justified; and second, that which can be regarded as colonization or development lines and which the railway could neither construct nor operate without assurance that its losses would not have to be borne through its ordinary operations.
Unquestionably the line to which the hon. gentleman refers, as well as others which have been mentioned this evening, with the possible exception of the P.G.E. extension-and I take it that these remarks will apply also to other representations which will be made this evening-fall within the first category. That being so, the railways have come to the conclusion that unless the particular new con-

struction can be justified economically, it would not be advisable at this time to proceed with it. They have come to that conclusion, not only because of the acute shortage of steel, but also for other reasons which it would take too long for me to go into at this time. I wanted to tell the hon. gentleman that his particular representations had not been forgotten, and the position at the present time is as I have outlined it. I trust it will be possible in later months to amend the decision.

Before bringing to the attention of the committee, Mr. Chairman, two matters which I wish to discuss briefly this evening, I must say it did my heart good to hear my good private-enterprise friend, the hon. member for Comox-Alberni, advocating the extension of the area of public ownership and public service. I know what he has to say with regard to the establishment of a coastguard service has the support of the people in British Columbia. What he said this evening represents, without doubt, the opinions of the people of that province.
I now want to deal for just a moment or two with the steamer service in the Iiootenays. I refer to Arrow and Kootenay lakes. I know what I am>
talking about, because I have lived on those lakes for forty-two years and I have travelled on those steamers for forty-two years. I remember the days when we had a fine fleet of steamers, the Rossland, the Kootenay, the Bonnington, the Sicamous, the Minto, the Moyie, the Kuskanook, and several smaller craft, handling car barges.
Today our service on the Arrow lakes is reduced to the steamer Minto, built in 1898, and on the Kootenay lake to the steamer Moyie, built during the same year. In fact I might say that these two stern-wheelers are the only steamers of their type operating today in the Dominion of Canada.
During recent years we have suffered from a decline of service on the lakes, while at the same time the population and the production of wealth have been increasing. This inland steamer service is actually the orphan of transportation in Canada. I took up the matter with the transport board and the minister; and I am informed that the federal government has no jurisdiction or responsibility with respect to these steamers, so far as service is concerned. I took up the matter with the provincial government officials and they said they had no responsibility with respect to service, so that we do not know where we stand. When it comes to the question of operating under the shipping act and certain other laws, and when it comes to the question of labour relations, both the dominion government and the Canadian Pacific recognize these trans-

Supply-Transport
portatioa services as national in character. But when it comes to bringing this transportation system under the jurisdiction of the transport board we are told by the minister and the board that it comes within the provincial sphere because the services are definitely within one province, while at the same time they are part of the Canadian Pacific railway system. It is not a coastal service nor an ocean service, but is a part of the Canadian Pacific railway system.
During the past year we had a heavy movement of fruit and other farm produce. If we had not been most fortunate in having the services of one of the finest skippers who ever sailed the lakes, Captain Estabrook, a great deal of the hay,, particularly, would not have been moved out before the small craft were put on the lower lakes. That skipper was able to continue operating later in the year than at any time in the last thirty years, by lining the steamer up the swift water by means of a winch and cable. But toward the end of the year the water became so low that the larger steamer had to cease operations on the lower lake, and for a distance of fifty miles all the isolated ranchers and communities were served, as far as passenger service is concerned, by a little launch brought in on a flat car by the Canadian Pacific, a launch which operated all winter without heat. It was a gasoline launch, and, l am informed, was not permitted to have a heating system. You can imagine the situation on a stormy winter night, with many of the passengers not accustomed to that type of tiavel, having to make a trip for a distance of perhaps fifty miles in a small launch, without heat. As far as freight service was concerned, they brought in a dinky tug, also on a flat car' It was so lacking in power that it could not handle a barge in stormy weather, and waited for fine days in order to do the work required.
The people of the Arrow lakes are not satisfied with the service they have been getting.
hey believe that this interior boat service should be brought under the jurisdiction of the transport board, and that they should have a better sendee. I know the Canadian Pacific have given consideration to building a new and somewhat larger steamer. I also know the cost of a new boat is very high compared with the cost some years ago. I happen to know that the steamer Minto was built in 1898 for about $48,000. I understand now that to build a steamer not a great deal larger but somewhat longer and wider in beam, and capable of carrying cars, will cost over half a million dollars. I realize those difficulties but I wish to bring to the attention of the minister the plight of the people on the lakes. At the present time, construction has commenced
on a $5,000,000 power plant on the Arrow lakes, which will mean the moving of an immense amount of construction material, supplies, equipment and so on. So I want to express to the minister once more the need for improved steamer service on the Arrow lakes, and the desire of the people to have this service brought under the jurisdiction of the transport board.
Perhaps that is sufficient for that subject this evening, but before concluding I should like to deal with a matter brought before the house originally this session, I believe by the hon. member for Kamloops. I believe he mentioned something about electrical fences of some sort for warning engineers and train crews of rock slides on the mountain divisions 1 do not remember the details-

ueieciur iences.

First I should like to correct a statement made by the hon. member for Royal, who said the people of the maritime provinces had helped build the Hudson Bay railway. The Hudson Bay railway was built with money received from the sale of some 14,085,880 acres of western Canadian land which sold for $42,257,640; and the people of Canada did not put up one nickel toward the building of that railway.
Earlier this evening the hon. member for Battle River referred again to the question of the gap between Heinsburg to Frenchman s Butte, and St. Walburg and Beaver River. This question has come before the house m

the last two sessions, and has had a thorough airing. One hon. member particularly has made a number of eloquent pleas for the people of that district. I refer to the hon. member for Athabaska.
In the last session the minister gave us some consideration and a little hope that something would be done in the near future. I am somewhat disappointed that as yet this session the hon. member for Athabaska has not seen fit to bring the matter again before the house. The people there are pretty well disappointed, and I hope the minister will have more encouragement for us this year than he did last.
I have here a letter from a lady in that constituency who went there a good many years ago, which I believe aptly describes the conditions in which many of these people have found themselves. I Shall take the time of the committee to place at least a part of the letter on record. This letter written by Mrs. Edith Gould, who signs herself as one of the lonesome pioneers, is dated at Iron Springs, Saskatchewan, and states:
Dear Sir:
We are living in a place which in 1933 promised to be a thriving community, when the railway seemed to be in the building and this was marked a townsite on the railway map. It was quickly settled with 36 settlers. Two stores opened up, a church and a school were built and we had our own post office. We all liked it here, and intended to stay and make good. But the war and hard times shut down the railway *works. Lack of money to work with and lack of implements to work with made many leave to seek work; also bad roads. The wax took some of the boys and younger men. And finally it was hard to get a teacher and the school was closed; and the remaining families had to move to town to get schooling for their children.
The buildings on this land are going to ruin. Some of them were good buildings which cost money to build, wells and fences are breaking, and all going back. The little church and school and other buildings are m danger of being destroyed, if a fire comes. It seems to me this is wilful neglect, for surely with so many people seeking a place to live and the cost ot living rising every day these homes could be made use of, and the district become a thriving one when the railway comes. It is a sad sight to see places where people had worked so hard to make a home, not just for a short time but for years. Now all are going to rum.
Although this letter is three or four pages in length, I shall not put any more of it on record. I do say, however, that these people are deserving of more consideration than thev are getting.	Because of the war and the
shortage of steel, it is possible that the government and the railways have had a good excuse in the past. But surely the situation as regards steel is greatly improved, and it is time that we gave to these people

Supply-Transport
some hope for the completion of that railway. I trust the minister will tell us tonight whether there is any hope, or not.

I am afraid I cannot add anything to what I said in reply to the hon. member for Swift Current, further than to say this, if it will give the hon. member any encouragement, 'that the line he refers to, namely, filling the gap between St. Wal-burg and Bonnyville, and Heinsburg and Frenchman's Butte, falls within the first class to which I referred a moment ago, namely that which the railway feels it should recommend on the basis of improving or rounding ' out the system, and serving the territories now without service, and which lines can be economically justified. While I am not in a position to say this is a line which can be economically justified, I hope it can be. I indicated as much to the delegation which waited upon me last year in western Canada. And while the railway committee which was eet up to deal with all these branch lines has not yet come to a conclusion with reference to it, perhaps because steel is in short supply, when the committee does go into the matter fully, while I am not able to tell the hon. member what the conclusion will be,
I would think it falls clearly within the first oa'tegory. From what I know of it, personally, I would also think it is one which can be economically justified.

I should like to add my support to the suggestions made by the hon. member for Shelburne-Yarmouth-Clare and the hon. member for Cornox-Aiberni. These statements had reference to *the coastguard service on the east and west coast. I would suggest to the minister an idea to improve this service, which I feel could be carried out without any great cost.
From previous experience I have had with the different departments, I have found 'that there appeared to be little co-operation between departments, so far as the amalgamation of services is concerned. The point I had in mind', however, has to do with the situation which prevails at the present time at Grand Manan island. At the present time the fisheries patrol boat, the Gannet Rock requires replacement. I thought that when this matter of replacement was being considered, the Department of Transport and 'the Department of Fisheries could get together and decide that a boat could be built and manned by a crew which would look after the interests, 'both of the Department of
Fisheries and the Department of Transport. At the same time it could act as a lifesaving boat.
The boat now employed by the Department of Transport at Grand Manan island for this purpose is an old lobster boat, about fifteen years old, powered by an automobile engine. Both the boat and the motor have outlived their usefulness. I saw this equipment as recently as last fall and I know that it is unfit for the job it is supposed to do, and that with very little expenditure of money this service could be improved.
In and around Grand Manan island one finds a rugged coast line with off-shore ledges and shoals which offer great danger to the fisherman. It is absolutely necessary that the lifesaving equipment be available at all times, and it could be used as well for the transportation of patients to hospitals on the mainland. It has often been found necessary, in the event of accidents or emergency surgical cases, to take patients to mainland hospitals, a considerable distance away. If the proper type of equipment were made available for each of these services, both for lifesaving and for fisheries patrol, it would be costly, and I believe that to some extent it would be criticized by the people on the island. If two boats and two crews were made available to look after the service I am certain that often one would find both boats and both crews doing nothing. That has happened often. But one boat could be built to take care properly of both services, with a full-time crew to look after the protection of the fishermen and the interests of the fisheries department. I believe that there would then be very little criticism and that many dollars could be saved in this way. If the Department of Fisheries and the Department of Transport would co-operate in this way it would eliminate much expenditure and would give the people a service which I feel they must have in order to carry on.
In making this suggestion to officials of the fisheries department, I was informed that they would object to a dual service, but so far they have not given any reasonable explanation why the two departments could not work together. In discussing the proposed service with officials of the transport department, I got the very same response, that it would not work out successfully to have the two departments controlling the one boat. Regardless of this fact, I am suggesting that the two departments do get together before any new equipment is furnished for either service on Grand Manan island and discuss intelligently the idea of having the two services performed by one boat, well equipped, and one crew, to
Supply-Transport

be controlled by both departments. In this way a better type of boat and equipment would be justified and a better service could be maintained. The cost of operation would be greatly reduced, and I think the department would be justified in maintaining the crew the year round.
The hon. member for Shelburne-Yarmouth-
Clare, speaking on this subject on May 14, suggested that we utilize all the available equipment we have in the fisheries department and the transport department. I heartily agree with his suggestion, and at the same time I suggest that in any planning done in future for improving the existing services favourable consideration be given to a combined service whereby the transport department and the Department of Fisheries may work together.
My reason for suggesting that the service might be controlled by the fisheries department is that the fisheries department have officials and offices scattered all over the maritime provinces, and, I think on the west coast too, whereas, the Department of Transport have few offices in comparison. They have one in Saint John city and another in Halifax, but their offices are not nearly as numerous as those of the Department of Fisheries.
I trust that the minister will give this matter his careful consideration, and in a case like Grand Manan I feel sure that a service could be inaugurated by the two departments which would give the fishermen coastguard protection, and at the same time the crew and boat would be available to look after the interests of the Department of Fisheries.

Mr. Chairman, I wish to support the well-expressed views of the hon. member for Royal and the hon. member for Cumberland in favour of the construction of the Chignecto canal. It is not my intention to speak on that matter this evening; I have spoken on it on other occasions, but I would say to the minister it is a live subject in the maritime provinces and it will continue to be a live subject until it is shown that the cost of construction is out of all proportion to the benefits that would be derived. If the matter is looked at both from the defence point of view and the commercial point of view, that will be a rather difficult thing to show.
I rise for the purpose of asking the minister a question. representations made by the premiers are still under active and careful study by the government. No decision has yet been arrived at. When one is reached, it will be announced.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, the various divisions of the minister's department are numerous indeed. I wish to talk about another phase of the work that comes within his department. I have in mind air services, which have only recently come directly under his ministerial jurisdiction.
As the minister knows, I have raised a particular question having to do with air services three times in the last two weeks. Naturally, if I had had an answer that was satisfactory to me I would not be raising the question again, but that is not the case.
As the minister knows, the government's policy with respect to international air services has been categorical and definite for a number of years. It began with a statement made by the Prime Minister on April 2, 1943. So far as international air services were concerned, the crux of his statement is to be found on pages 1777 and 1778 of Hansard of that date. It was to the effect that all air services across international boundaries or from Canada to other countries would be performed, so far as Canada's operation was concerned, by the government agency, namely, TransnCanada Air Lines. That policy was spelled out and reiterated by the present

Supply-Transport
Minister of Trade and Commerce a year later. His speech was made on March 17, 1944, and the significant part of that speech is to be found at page 1579 of Hansard of that date. He reiterated the Prime Minister's announcement of the year before, making it quite clear that it was the government's firm intention that all international services would be operated by Trans-Canada Air Lines.
In 1945, the next year, the matter was up again. It came up during the consideration of amendments to the Trans-Canada Air Lines Act. Those amendments had to do with subsidiary organizations under T.C.A., but in the discussion the present Minister of Trade and Commerce, who was then in charge of this matter, made it clear that the government was adhering to its policy that all international air services would be operated by the chosen instrument, namely Trans-Canada Air Lines. Again, in the next year, 1946, this policy was reiterated by the minister then in charge and again he spelled it out, this time with special reference to the proposal to establish an air service between this country and Australia. The particular spelling out to which I refer is found at page 5640 of Hansard of August 30,
1946.	On that date the minister announced an agreement between Canada and Australia and said that, so far as the Canadian end of the agreement is concerned, it would be operated by Trans-Canada Air Lines.
Again last year, 1947, there were discussions of this matter on the estimates and the policy of the government was reiterated. As I say, in all these five years, 1943, 1944, 1945, 1946 and
1947,	the policy has been just as definite as it could be laid down. It was absolute and categorical. There was no reluctance on the part of the government to state its policy; there was no suggestion to anyone in this house that government policy would be announced in due course.
Some members of the house did not like the policy. We in this group did, but whatever the reactions to it we all knew what that policy was in language that we clearly understood. A few weeks ago, however, there began to appear in some of the newspapers of this country suggestions that we might expect a change in policy with respect, in particular, to the service across the Pacific. I was concerned, partly because I approved the announced policy of the government and disapproved the idea that this service should be turned over to Canadian Pacific Air Lines or to any private company. I was also disturbed because it seemed to me that this kind of thing has happened too often. We have had an understanding as to what government policy was with 5849-255
respect to one matter or another. Rumours have appeared in the press that a change was in the offing. We have asked our questions here in the house and have been brushed off, and then in due course the rumours are confirmed. I will not take the time to indicate in detail some of the examples. I could refer to dominion government annuities, which is in another department, or I could refer to the discussions we had a couple of years ago when the government changed its policy in the matter of railways owning and operating air lines. At any rate, because of these rumours that a change was pending, I directed a question to the Minister of Reconstruction and Supply on Thursday, May 6, 1948, as recorded at page 3653 of Hansard. My question had two parts, but I will deal at this moment only with the second part, in which I asked:
Is it still government policy that when this service is put into effect by Canada it will be by the government-owned air line, and not by any private company.
The reply made by the Minister of Reconstruction and Supply to that part of my question was in these words:
So far as government policy is concerned, I dare say when the matter is considered the government will be able to announce its policy.
I went on, and asked:
Has there been any change?
But I got no answer to that supplementary question.
To me that exchange seemed to underline some of the rumours that I had heard about a change in policy, because never before, at least not since 1943, had there been any reluctance on the part of the government or of any of its ministers to state its policy in this field quite clearly. Therefore, at the first opportunity, namely, when the house was asked to go into supply on Monday, May 10, I raised the matter again. I felt, to use language that hon. members will understand, that I was leading with my chin, sticking my neck out and going out on a limb in asking the question that I put to the .minister. I quite expected that he would slap me down- that is, the Minister of Trade and Commerce- in his own inimitable fashion.

If the minister will make a statement with regard to the board of transport commissioners and the question of branch lines I feel sure that will be helpful to members who have these problems in their constituencies. The problem which I have to present is unique, I think, in the fact that I believe it will require for its solution the co-operation of both the large railway companies of Canada. There are some thousands of square miles of agricultural territory west of Yorkton that are fairly well developed, with a number of villages along two spur lines, in which the people are today in receipt of a sort of dead-end service which is inadequate to meet the situation. It seriously iso-
[Mr. Chevrier.J
lates these people; and they feel it severely and have been somewhat concerned about the situation for a number of years.
These spur lines were built in the heyday of railway construction in the west, when the two railway companies were trying to head each other off. The line running out of Yorkton to Parkerview was built by the Canadian National to head off the Canadian Pacific from coming into that territory. The Canadian Pacific went into Foam Lake and ran a branch line southward, to cut off development by the Canadian National from Foam Lake to Wishart. I do not believe that those two branch lines should be penalized because of the action in those days.
The people have been searching for some kind of solution and some constructive suggestions which they might make with regard to coming to some solution. Boards of trade, rural municipalities, and village councils have had meetings. After discussing the matter, they thought probably a petition from the people in that area might help. Today I am in receipt of several hundred more signatures. They are coming to my desk frequently and will be forwarded to the minister when they have all arrived. I should like to point out what the petition asks for. It reads as follows:
The petition of the undersigned citizens of the Dominion of Canada humbly shew'eth:
That the present situation with regard to passenger, mail and freight service on the Yorkton-Parkerview, Canadian National Railways branch, and the Foam Lake-Wishart, Canadian Pacific Railway branch, is completely inadequate to serve the residents in those areas, who are dependent on these branches for railway services ;
And that the rail-way companies have failed to provide improved services on the grounds that it is too costly under existing arrangements on spur lines;
And that we believe that the production and population in this area warrants improved railway facilities;
Wherefore your petitioners humbly pray that the Canadian Pacific Railway, the Canadian National Railways, and the board of transport commissioners, and the Department of Transport do immediately undertake the solution to this problem, to which end we humbly submit this plan:
(1)	One or other of these companies purchase the right of way, and other properties belonging to the other railway;
(2)	Then by joining up the two branches and continuing the construction of the railway either to Wynyard, or some other point on the Canadian Pacific Railway, or Raymore or some other point on the Canadian National Railways, proper through service can be provided to the residents of this area of Saskatchewan from Yorkton to the other terminating point.
I do not know what the possibilities are, how far the minister can go or to what length the board of transport commissioners can go.

But since the minister has set up this committee he spoke about this evening, it seems to me that, through such an organization as that, the two companies could investigate the possibilities of each one buying out the other's rights, and then by joining up the two, giving a through service.

So that there will not be any misunderstanding, may I tell the hon. gentleman that the committee I referred to a moment ago was not a committee of the board of transport commissioners. It is a committee of the Canadian National Railways that are studying the whole question of branch lines. They have reported, as I mentioned a moment ago, that they placed all branch lines in two categories.

Yes, thank you. There are possibilities, however, of similar committees on the Canadian Pacific. I think it will require the getting together of the two companies in order to bring about a solution of this particular problem. I trust that the minister will have looked into and reported on the possibility of some such solution as this. I can assure him that he can certainly have from any of the members all possible assistance, and the appreciation of the people who live in that area, who believe that something could be done along these lines. If the possibilities could be investigated, that would be as much as I would ask at this time. I will let the minister have the petition.
I shall be glad to have it,

I wish to refer for a moment or two to something that was said by members from the maritime provinces, namely, with regard to the proposed Chignecto canal. One of the hon. members, I have forgotten which one it was, hinted at the strategic importance of the proposed canal. As the minister knows, I have spent considerable time in that area, and I plan to spend some more there next summer.
Since last session I have been carrying on a survey, mostly by correspondence, all over the world as to strategic canals. I have arrived at the conclusion that, besides the importance of the proposed Chignecto canal, from a commercial point of view, it is of great importance to Canada, an importance that is increasing more and more as the world foreign picture changes; that is, it is getting more and more important strategically.
The minister knows of a number of canals. There is the Corinth canal which is about four miles in length. It cuts across the isthmus of Corinth in the south of Greece.
That canal likely could not be justified in any other way than as a strategic canal, although it is an important commercial link. As far as the kingdom of Greece is concerned, it is of immense importance strategically. That country did not hesitate to put it through. It is a sea-level canal, and it goes through a deep cut, about 100 feet, I believe, at the most. It can be justified om that account.
Then the Italian government built what was called the Victor Emmanuel III canal. That canal, too, is a strategic one. It is some twelve miles long, and has a depth of thirty-two feet.
I should have said that the Corinth canal has a depth of twenty-six feet.
Then in the United States for many years there was an agitation, just the same as our maritime friends have had, for a canal across the isthmus at Cape Cod. I would suggest that, when the occasion presents itself, the minister should send his engineering brigade to Cape Cod-that is not far away-and let them examine what was done there. That canal is seventeen miles long. It, too, is a sea-level canal. There is a tide at each end of from four to six feet, and there is a current of some five to six knots. That was just not the easiest engineering problem to overcome, but a sea-level canal was put through at Cape Cod which, during the war, was of vital importance to the United States. It likely saved thousands of lives and many ships. It means to the United States just the same as the canal across the Chignecto isthmus would mean to Canada, from a strategic point of view.
Then the minister perhaps knows about the Chesapeake-Delaware canal, from the Chesapeake river to the Delaware river. That canal is eighteen miles long and has a depth of thirty-five feet. It was not the easiest canal in the world to build, but it, too, is a sea-level canal between those two rivers. It is important to the United States.
Everyone knows of the Kiel canal. That, too, is a sea-level canal, sixty-one miles long, from the North sea to the Baltic sea. That was built by the Germans, and is also a strategic canal.
Then there is the Suez canal built by the British. That canal is 100 miles long. It was not so hard perhaps to build, because it was built through sand, but it has been of vast important to the British empire as a strategic canal.
Our United States friends built the present Panama canal, which has many locks. I am not going to refer to that particularly, but it is also a strategic canal and no doubt is rapidly paying for itself. They are now planning on building a sea-level canal across that isthmus
Supply-Transport

at a cost of perhaps $500 million. On the west side they have a twenty-foot tide to contend with. That is not as bad as Chignecto, where the tide is still higher. I appreciate the difficulty presented by the tide of the bay of Fundy in connection with the Chignecto canal; but our United States cousins are planning on a gigantic lock at the west end of the proposed new Panama canal, into which ships will come when sailing east, and out of which they will sail into the Pacific ocean when going west.
I am going to point out that today the question of strategy is so important that I could understand the Chignecto canal being built by the Department of National Defence, so that the minister's department would not be charged with 'building a commercial canal, which I would support. I associate myself with what has been said this evening by the hon. member for Cumberland, the hon. member for Royal, and the hon. member for St. John-Albert. As a commercial undertaking, I am sure the Chignecto canal would be a success, but there can be no argument whatever as to its success as a strategic canal. The minister can see that as well as anyone else. I recognize the problems that must be faced, but perhaps we could take the matter off the shoulders of the minister and transfer it to national defence. It is a matter of vital national importance to this country, and during the last war many lives would have been saved if that canal had been constructed.
The United States has expressed her willingness to co-operate with Canada in building the St. Lawrence seaway; at least the proposal has not yet been killed in the United States senate. That being so, I suggest that they might welcome the opportunity, if we wished to let them in on it, to co-operate with us in building this canal as a continental defence measure. I do not make that suggestion; perhaps it would be going much too far, but since we are co-operating with them in defence matters in the north, here is a canal just as vitally important to the defence of the United States as to the defence of Canada, and to my knowledge that point has never been emphasized.

I refer to Dufferin street, which is an old county road and which will v "come a main artery as far north as Orillia. In 
Toronto it runs right down to the main entrance of the Canadian National exhibition grounds. I am not so sure that the department has not already looked into the question.
Yes; the application is before the board.

I am very glad. That
shows how I keep in touch with these matters. I try to do so, but, as someone said earlier tonight, we are not always advised of these applications and do not know of them.

Of course you could
not expect me to be other than in favour of the Dufferin street subway, because that is a main north to south artery in Davenport riding. I seldom mention anything about my riding because I am trying to help the w'hole of Canada, in the firm belief that the more I can do for all Canada outside Toronto, the more I am doing for Toronto. I realize that the city of Toronto depends upon the rest of Canada, that the prosperity of the rest of Canada means the prosperity of Toronto; and I have often said there is no better way I can help my riding or the city as a whole than by seeing the rest of Canada prosper and expand. In this case, however, the subway would be in Davenport riding. I do not believe I have asked in this house for a public works for my riding as long as I have been here; I can hardly get down to that kind of stuff only. However, I leave that thought with the .minister. I am glad to know the matter is under consideration, and I very much appreciate his kindness in telling me so.

You did not ask me.

Supply-Transport
The matter I have in mind definitely concerns my riding and, unlike the hon. member for Davenport, I have no hesitation in speaking about such matters.
What is your riding?

I have occasionally mentioned the name here: Fraser Valley. I was elected here with or in spite of the assistance of the hon. member for Vancouver North, and I am going to speak on behalf of my riding and on a matter in which I am personally concerned.
It is a personal matter, not like whaling?

If margarine is
finished I shall carry on.
Whale oil.

I would not go so far as to say whale oil; there is only personal profit in that.
In my riding we have a branch of the Canadian Pacific railway running a distance of 10-1 miles from Mission to Huntingdon. I took up this matter with the minister on his estimates last year, and I am going to quote from a letter he wrote me following the discussion at that time. This branch of the railroad runs behind a dike protecting the land from floods on the Fraser river, which at the present time are rather serious; yet the Canadian Pacific has never paid five cents in diking tax for this protection. I am going to quote this letter, because it shows that the president of the Canadian Pacific Railway Company was either deliberately giving the minister false information, or that he was misinformed. I want to place this on record because I was not permitted to rise a few minutes ago, and as a result this debate will certainly not be finished by eleven o'clock. Under date of November 3, 1947, the minister wrote me as follows:
The Mission subdivision extends from the main line at Mission, B.C., southerly for a distance of 10-1 miles to Huntingdon. It was placed in operation in June, 1891, that is, prior to the construction of the Matsqui dyke. The company from time to time has been requested to contribute toward the cost of the Matsqui dyke, but has consistently refused on the ground that the dyke does not benefit the lands of the railway company. Under the drainage, dyking and development act of British Columbia provision is made for the exclusion from a dyking district of lands not benefited. In 1895 a court of revision, because the company's land did not benefit, exempted the company from assessments in connection with the dyke.
The only grade revision on the subdivision took place in 1912, when a long timber trestle
was replaced. As a result of the replacement, the track was lowered approximately five feet for a distance of approximately three thousand feet. This grade revision was in no way dependent upon or connected1 with any dyke or other protective facility.
I could go on reading from this letter, but I wish to point out to the minister that either the president of the Canadian Pacific Railway Company was misinforming the minister, or he was ill-advised. I walked that distance in gum boots through two feet of water in the flood, and watched a locomotive go through under that water. Perhaps the minister could tell me how the president of the Canadian Pacific Railway Company is any way affected by this protection.
Perhaps I might give some facts and figures in connection with this. Mind you, this is a railway with millions of dollars invested in it, and making millions of dollars too. It was the best of all the lines they had during the war- all the lines of the Canadian Pacific Railway Company. It has never paid five cents in protection.
Here are the actual figures, and I defy the minister-I must correct myself; I was going to say his friends-I defy the minister or those gentlemen of the Canadian Pacific who gave these either deliberately falsified or misdirected statements. Here are the levels of this branch of railway from Huntingdon to Mission. The dike was constructed, after the break-in in 1904 or near that date, to an elevation of 28-37. Here are the flood levels:

1894	 26-37
1921	 22-70

I ask the committee to take note of these levels of the Canadian National Railways, top of rail. These are the railways we own, that the people of Canada own. And I draw attention to the point where they cross the Canadian Pacific railway. Mark you, this is the Canadian National Railways, with millions of dollars invested in it. And I alone have paid over $300 a year diking tax. The level at Gifford is 24-15; at pump No. 1, 22-9; at Diamond, where is crosses the Canadian Pacific, it is 24-57.
And I will just give the point where Cruick-shank pays $300 on his own farm at the township road, where it is 21-8, and the flood was at 22-35 in that area.
The minister has the courage to send a letter such as that from the Canadian Pacific to me, and then to tell me that we should have an increase in freight rates of 21 per cent.
Supply-Transport

because the Canadian Pacific treat all parts of Canada fairly, and because they assume their full obligations in all parts of Canada! The fact is that right today we are very much afraid, on account of the climatic conditions in the coast this year, that we may have another flood.
No government since I have been connected with politics, and long before, has had the courage to say to the Canadian Pacific where they should go and what they should do. May I say I am disappointed in the attitude the government has taken in this matter to date. I am sorry I have not all the information with me, showing what the board of transport commissioners have said. I would very much like to read it all. I know the minister does not know all this, because I know him very well and I do not think for one moment that he would permit the Canadian Pacific to dictate to this or any other government, as they are dictating at the present time.
I am sorry to take up further time, but-and it is all very well for some of my hon. friends to laugh; but this is a serious matter for the farmers in my district.
Just convince the minister.

I know where the hon. member for Vancouver Bast would be in this, because his party feel as keenly about this as I do, so far as that particular area is concerned. I might even get a little support from the hon. member for Vancouver North if I talk long enough.
He is for you now-a free trader, and a great Liberal.
I seem to get a great deal of assistance when I make a speech around here. But those who cannot tell the story on behalf of their own districts envy one who can speak on behalf of his district.
And so clearly, too.
I could come back on that, but I think I had better not.
You had better adjourn the debate.

I will say this, that I represent the farmers in my riding, and to the best of my ability I think I make a pretty good job of it. I do not need any assistance
or interruptions from those who spend most of their time in visiting outside the house, and who do not stay here to fight on behalf of their constituents.
I say it is a disgrace to this government or any other government to permit a railway to avoid taxation. Mark you, this is a revenue producing line, making many millions of dollars, and we farmers have to pay for it. The last time the dike was wrecked the Canadian National was out for forty-eight hours. The hon. member from the Vancouver district who has been interrupting knows that just as well as I do; and that affects not only Fraser valley, but the whole of British Columbia,
For the railway company through the minister to submit to me a letter stating that they are not affected at all, after I have set out their levels and have told them that their railway was under two feet of water; for them to tell me that it is not a matter of national concern and that they should be allowed a free hand, in the face of this 21 per cent freight increase, and when they can pay only seven cents an hour increase in wages, is not good enough.
I would ask that it be called eleven o'clock, and that the minister prepare a statement for me when we resume again.
Item stands. -
Progress reported.
What is the business for tomorrow?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Tomorrow we shall resume the debate on the second reading of Bill No. 300, to amend the Canada Shipping Act, 1934. If that bill is passed we shall go into committee of supply to continue the estimates of the Minister of Transport. At eight o'clock, as previously announced, the Minister of Finance will bring down his budget. I understand that the budget debate will be adjourned by a member of the opposition. Then, if the Minister of Transport has not concluded his shipping bill or his estimates, he will continue. If this work is completed we shall resume debate on the second reading of Bill No. 280, to amend the National Housing Act, 1944.
At eleven o'clock the house adjourned, without question put, pursuant to standing order.
Tuesday, May 18, 1948
